author: groganz-bot[bot]
body:
**In simple words:** a design pin (the recorded revision of the source drawings the product's lifecycle screens are built to) can silently fall behind the drawings it claims to follow, and the eight owner-drawn anchors the acceptance suite is supposed to check against those drawings do not actually resolve today. This change adds three CI checks that make both facts visible and enforceable, plus the future pin-move script (not run here).

### G1 — design-pin-freshness

`scripts/ci/design-pin-freshness.mjs` asks the design source, over the REST API with the same App-installation credential road the existing pin-drift check already mints, whether any revision touching a governed drawing path landed after the pin. It warn-annotates on every pull request and turns red on a push to main and on a pull request touching a mapped lifecycle path. With no credential, a refused read, a failed read, or an unreadable answer it fails closed (exit 2) rather than passing silently. Its public message names only the pin id and the two files in this repository that carry it — no revision, no path, no count, no date, and the whole disclosure bound is pinned by a suite assertion that its output carries no digit at all.

### G4 — design-anchor-resolution

`scripts/ci/design-anchor-resolution.mjs` recomputes every `ownerAnchors` selector and every capture requirement live from the recorder, and checks whether each one resolves — by exact attribute match — in the drawing bytes the pin governs at the pin's own revision. It reports resolved, unresolved, and refused (an unsupported selector form) per anchor, naming only which governed drawing (by position, never by path) resolved it. Measured read-only against the real pinned drawings outside this repository: all 8 recorded owner anchors are unresolved today, plus two selector forms this checker refuses outright. That is the true state and this gate now reports it truthfully in warn mode.

### G3 — design-record-grammar

`scripts/ci/design-record-grammar.mjs` requires every Fix-leg / capture-graded section of a pull request body to carry a `design@` token followed by a 40-hex value equal to the branch's own pin, naming both values when a section disagrees.

### G0 — the adoption road (written, not applied)

`scripts/audit/adopt-design-pin.mjs` performs the future pin move as one rolled-back transaction: it edits both pin-bearing documents textually, records the sorted unresolved set from G4, and takes the digest only from the canonical `--print-anchor-digest` script, rolling the whole tree back if either reader fails. It is fixture-tested but was not run against this repository's own files — the pin values in both documents are byte-identical to origin/main. The anchor contract gained `anchorsUnresolvedAtPin` as a present-only fourth digest input: absent, the digest is unchanged from today; once recorded it cannot be edited without moving the digest. Recorded == recomputed digest is unchanged on this branch.

### Suites, gates, typecheck

131 new tests across four suites (freshness, anchor-resolution, record-grammar, adoption) all green; the untouched sibling pin-drift suite (49 tests) green; the anchor-contract, acceptance-gate and binding suites unaffected and green; `node scripts/ci/product-tree-hygiene.mjs` clean; `authz:inventory:check` clean; `node scripts/audit/ci-pinned-tests-exist.mjs` green; typecheck zero errors in the product tree; eslint clean on every touched file. A mechanical leak scan over every added line is clean.

### Convergence

One read-only round found 12 issues; 8 were fixed with new red-first tests (a partial anchor set escaping the adoption road when a selector is refused, a disclosure leak on the freshness gate's clean-path message, an unreadable pull-request body silently read as absent, `git diff` failures escaping the guard around `git rev-parse`, the ATX heading grammar not matching indented headings or tracking fence-marker length, attribute-name case folding, an unresolved anchor worded as a negative when only governed drawings were read, the recorded unresolved set never compared against what the check finds, and the textual JSON field edits taking the first occurrence anywhere in a large prose document instead of the record itself); 2 were rebutted with the issue text as the counter-evidence (the pin-bearing files are deliberately left untouched — that is this task's own scope; and G3/G4 naming their own recorded values is what the issue's own grammar and disclosure rules require).

### Workflow wiring (not in this PR)

`.github/workflows/**` is a protected path for this change and is not touched here. The three jobs still need wiring into the gates workflow, matching the existing pin-drift job's shape (checkout at fetch-depth 0 with persist-credentials false, Node 24, no install step), with the freshness and anchor-resolution jobs also minting the same design-source read token the existing pin-drift job mints (continue-on-error true on the mint step, so a missing credential still lets each checker report its own closed failure rather than aborting the job silently) and the record-grammar job needing no credential at all, since it reads only the pull request body already in the event payload.

```
design-pin-freshness:
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  timeout-minutes: 10
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout with fetch-depth 0, persist-credentials false
    - uses: actions/setup-node with node-version 24
    - name: Mint the design-source read token
      id: design-token
      continue-on-error: true
      uses: actions/create-github-app-token (same inputs as the pin-drift job's mint step)
    - name: Design Pin Freshness
      env:
        DESIGN_SOURCE_TOKEN: (the minted token output)
      run: node scripts/ci/design-pin-freshness.mjs --github-annotations (with the same base-resolution block the pin-drift step already uses)

design-anchor-resolution: same shape and same mint step, final line node scripts/ci/design-anchor-resolution.mjs --github-annotations

design-record-grammar: same shape without the mint step, final line node scripts/ci/design-record-grammar.mjs --github-annotations
```

Credential requirement: the App installation must cover the design source with contents:read for the two credentialed checkers to run past a closed failure.

author: luchoc-dev
body:
Closes #187. Task 5 of phase 11d, which asked for #56 to be resolved or given a written reason for staying open.

## The decision

**#56 stays open, and it is a phase of its own rather than a task of this one.** Not because the check is hard — the measurement below says it is cheaper than #56 assumed — but because **running it green today needs an audit pass over roughly fifteen real findings**, which is 10a's kind of work, not 11d's. Building the check is an afternoon; the phase is what comes after it turns red.

The question was worth asking rather than assuming, because 11d's own generator depends on `docs-refs` for its single known weak point: `tools/build-level-docs.js` quotes constants from `core/`, and regenerating cannot catch a drift there.

## The measurement

A prototype extractor over the 104 markdown files in scope — `docs/**/*.md` excluding `docs/sources/`, plus `README.md` and `CLAUDE.md`:

| | count |
|---|---|
| backticked spans in scope | 8,988 |
| shaped like a path | 1,937 (474 distinct) |
| shaped like a Java type | 2,218 (466 distinct) |
| neither | 4,833 |

**A naive extractor leaves 271 unresolved. A narrowed one leaves 122** — and the difference is entirely in the extractor, not in an allow-list, which is the trade #56 asked to be checked.

The single largest rule: **this repository names paths relative to the Java package** — `core/port/WaveEndCondition.java`, not the full `core/src/main/java/dev/luchoc/...` path — so resolution must be by suffix. That one change took unresolved paths from **155 to 50**.

Of the 122 left, **72 are types and almost all are libGDX or JDK names** — `Math`, `String`, `List`, `Gdx`, `Pixmap`, `SpriteBatch`, `Skin`, `JsonReader`, `Thread`, `ConcurrentHashMap`. About fifty names, a genuinely closed set. **That is the "short allow-list" #56 set as its bar.**

The 50 paths split five ways: more extraction work, build output, branch names with an unlisted prefix, the deliberate references to deleted things, and **about fifteen that are genuinely stale** — `core-deferred-surface.md`, `content-pipeline-design.md`, `boss-l1.json`, `specimen.png`, `game/ui/GameSkin`, `core/build.gradle`, and others. `docs-refs` would find real rot today. That group is the phase's actual content.

## The hard case, which #56 does not solve and should

`docs/plan/10a-honest-documentation/audit.md` and `mechanism.md` quote false references **on purpose**, because their subject is false references, and `docs/STATUS.md` does the same for `spikes/web-viability/` by 10a's own decision D1 — those citations *"are a dated record of a past phase and stay as written"*.

So the failure mode is not a missing name but **a document whose job is to name missing things**. #56 proposes an allow-list. **An allow-list keyed on the name is the wrong key:** `Composition.java` is legitimately absent in `audit.md` and would be a genuine finding in `12-architecture.md`, and one entry covers both. Whoever builds this decides between a per-file exemption and an inline marker **before** writing the extractor.

## The interaction task 1 flagged, answered

The contract warned that the generated level documents are dense with backticked content ids that look like references — `enemy-basic`, `l1-veteran-mix`, `slow-descent`.

author: vshcherb
body:
Fixes the `WARN: Native File not initialized from cache: /home/tileserver/maps/....obf` flood in the build log.

## Cause

`initAllMaps` opened every map with a plain `initMapFile`, so the native library never got an index cache: it warned once per map and re-read the index of all of them on every run.

## Fix

The tester now builds `indexes.cache` and hands it to `initCacheMapFile` before opening the maps. The cache goes into the **working folder** — `-cache.dir`, default `user.dir`, so on Jenkins it lands in `$WORKSPACE` and survives between builds — and never into the maps folder, which on a tile server is shared and may be read only.

Measured with 126 maps locally:

| | init | warnings |
|---|---|---|
| cold, no cache | 11.6 s | 0 |
| second run, cache reused | **2.4 s** | 0 |

The gain grows with the number of maps; the builder loads 1078.

## Two supporting changes in NativeJavaRendering

- `initIndexesCache` got an overload that takes the cache file explicitly. The existing three argument method still writes into the maps folder, so no other caller changes behaviour.
- **A broken obf no longer aborts the whole folder.** `Uruguay_southamerica_2.obf` in a local maps folder is corrupt, and going through the index cache turned that into a fatal `IOException: Corrupt file, it should have ended as it starts with version` that killed the entire run before a single tile was rendered. It is now logged and skipped, and also kept out of the list of maps to open. Worth a look during review — it changes shared behaviour, but one bad file killing a 1078 map scan seems clearly wrong.

```
SEVERE: Skipping map .../Uruguay_southamerica_2.obf: Corrupt file, ...
Indexes cache : .../indexes.cache (created)
Initialized 126 maps from /Users/.../maps
```

author: oakcask
body:
## Intent

Complete Workstream 6 by evaluating the full supported JSON Schema feature set against the immutable native graph, including ordered detailed errors, references, annotations, formats, and content assertions.

## Consequences

Forced-native validation now accepts every supported keyword instead of rejecting evaluation beyond the type slice. Native snapshots retain resource-root, dialect-policy, and dynamic-scope metadata. Each call uses independent evaluation state so compiled validators remain shareable across threads and Ractors. Native CI compares all 5,091 selected official-suite cases against the Ruby oracle in separate processes, and package smoke exercises a compound schema through the native backend. Interpreter and YJIT checkpoint samples are retained; they do not change the production default.

## Risks

The complete graph-view path currently has higher per-call overhead than the Ruby oracle in the retained checkpoint. Production-default selection remains deferred to Workstream 9, and the committed benchmark makes this regression observable. Custom meta-schema behavior depends on the compact dialect flags retained in each native node; the full differential corpus covers the current contract.

## Compliance and Revisit Triggers

Generated-source drift tests preserve deterministic output. Forced-native specs prohibit construction of the Ruby evaluator and cover keyword categories, detailed ordering, annotations, format/content options, lifecycle, GC, threads, and Ractors. The separate-process differential gate exposes backend identity or semantic divergence for every selected official case. Changes to evaluator semantics, dialect policy, graph metadata, the case catalog, or supported CRuby minors require rerunning these gates and the interpreter/YJIT checkpoint.

author: mattronix
body:
## Problem

The **Download ATAK overlay package** button saved a 0-byte `manet-topology-overlay.zip`.

## The backend is not at fault

`handleATAKPackage` needs no core data, so it can be exercised standalone. Running the binary directly and fetching the endpoint returns a valid archive:

```
HTTP 200 size=794

      486  MANIFEST/manifest.xml
      436  overlays/manet-topology.kml
```

`X-Overlay-Host` resolves correctly into the seed KML's NetworkLink:

```xml
<href>https://192.168.50.42/api/applets/atak-overlay/proxy/topology.kml</href>
<refreshInterval>15</refreshInterval>
```

`writeZip` also buffers, closes the zip writer, and only then writes — all correct.

## The bug

In `index.html`, the frontend blob download called:

```js
a.click();
a.remove();
URL.revokeObjectURL(url);   // synchronous
```

`URL.revokeObjectURL` ran synchronously immediately after `a.click()`, invalidating the object URL before the browser had finished reading the blob. The file that reached disk was empty. The revoke is now deferred so the download holds its reference first.

## Second defect fixed

`.then(function(r){ return r.blob(); })` never checked `r.ok`. A non-200 — the applet proxy's error when the backend is not running, or `handleTopologyKML`'s 502 when core is unreachable — was blobbed and saved as a `.zip` the user could not open, with no error shown. It now throws into the existing `catch` and alerts.

This matters in practice: the applet is currently installed but not running on the node, and `/etc/atak-overlay.conf` does not exist (only `atak-overlay.conf.default` in the applet dir), so this path is reachable today.

## Note

Not deployed to any node — frontend-only change, picked up on the next image deploy.

author: guyot-bertrand
body:
## Ce que #269 demandait, et ce qu'on a trouvé en le faisant

L'issue rapportait un symptôme : un commentaire ajouté au `Makefile` faisait
passer clang-tidy de 2 fichiers à 223, soit 72 s contre 827. La cause n'était
pas le `Makefile` — **clang-tidy ne l'a jamais lu.** Ce dont dépend le résultat
d'une unité de traduction est sa source, ses en-têtes transitifs, sa ligne de
commande de compilation, la configuration et le binaire. Les trois premiers, le
système de construction les connaît déjà, exactement et sans heuristique.

clang-tidy est donc accroché à la règle de compilation de chaque source, sous un
preset `tidy` — `cmake/Tidy.cmake`. Disparaissent `tidy-scope.sh` et ses
196 lignes, `TIDY_BASE`, la liste des « fichiers gouvernants », la fermeture
d'en-têtes par `grep` de nom de fichier, et le tableau de `CLAUDE.md` qui disait
ce que la porte lit.

### Mesuré, sur douze cœurs

| Situation | Ce qui est analysé |
| :--- | :--- |
| rien n'a changé | **0,4 s** — « ninja: no work to do » |
| un `.cpp` touché | **1** fichier |
| un en-tête profond touché | **129** fichiers — ses dépendants, et eux seuls |
| analyse complète | 5 min 37 |

`make check` passe de quarante minutes à **4 min 32**.

### Les deux entrées que Ninja ne voit pas

Le contenu de `.clang-tidy` et la version du binaire ne sont pas sur la ligne de
commande : les modifier ne rejouerait rien, et l'arbre resterait vert sur une
réponse périmée — **un mode d'échec plus discret que celui qu'on remplace**,
puisque l'ancien se trompait en analysant trop.

Leur empreinte va donc dans les **drapeaux de compilation**, et non dans les
arguments de clang-tidy : « la ligne de commande a changé donc je rejoue » est
propre à Ninja, alors que le générateur Makefile fait dépendre chaque objet de
son `flags.make`. La garantie vaut avec les deux, et le projet ne fige pas son
générateur.

Vérifié : configuration modifiée → **337 unités en attente** ; configuration
rétablie → **zéro**, sans rien réanalyser, puisque l'empreinte suit le contenu
et non la date.

Vérifié aussi que le filet ne prend que ce qu'il doit : **223 sources, exactement
celles de `src/`**. Les cinq `mocs_compilation.cpp` sont hors linting par le
`SKIP_LINTING` que CMake pose seul, Catch2 par une exemption explicite.

## `HeaderFilterRegex` n'avait jamais filtré

Le motif `src/.*\.hpp$` ne correspond à rien depuis la racine du dépôt, qui est
le répertoire courant que le `Makefile` imposait. **La porte n'a donc analysé
aucun en-tête depuis le début du projet.** Le preset l'a réglé par construction,
son répertoire courant étant l'arbre de construction.

Quarante-quatre diagnostics distincts en sont sortis :

| Traitement | Nb | Quoi |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| corrigés dans le code | 21 | casse des `constexpr`, ternaire imbriqué écrit à plat, parenthèses, paramètres inutilisés nommés en commentaire |
| deux options écrites | 12 | les cinq noms que `std::iterator_traits` impose ; les agrégats du modèle, qui portent leurs membres en clair par décision |
| un `NOLINTBEGIN` | 11 | la table des huit cadences — la définition d'une constante est le seul endroit où un littéral a le droit d'être nu |
| **un vrai défaut** | 1 | `TypedReference::target`, un `Timestamp` d'interface laissé non initialisé |

**Corollaire découvert au passage, et inscrit** : un `.clang-tidy` de répertoire
ne gouverne que les `.cpp` de ce répertoire. Pour un diagnostic levé dans un
en-tête, c'est la configuration de l'unité qui l'inclut qui s'applique — ceux de
`gui/` et de `test/` ne s'appliquaient donc pas à leurs propres en-têtes. C'est
la raison pour laquelle les deux exemptions locales sont des `NOLINT` et non des
options : un fichier de configuration ne pouvait pas les porter.

`readability-redundant-member-init` est désactivé, avec sa raison : il appelle
redondant un `{}` qui ne l'est pas — c'est l'initialisateur de membre par défaut,
et c'est lui qui rend légale l'initialisation désignée partielle. **Mesuré : sur
quinze retraits, trois sites d'appel ont cessé de compiler.**

## Le refactor a révélé une branche jamais éprouvée

Le ternaire imbriqué de `saturatedProduct` tenait ses quatre cas de signe sur une
ligne, si bien qu'un seul chemin suffisait à la marquer couverte. Écrite à plat,
la quatrième — gauche positif, droite négatif — s'est révélée sans test. Le
cliquet de couverture l'a vue passer de 1 à 2 lignes non couvertes ; elle a
désormais son cas, et le relevé est intact à 59.

## Les étapes sortent du Makefile

`src/scripts/gate/` porte treize étapes autonomes, `src/scripts/gate.sh` porte
l'ordre et sait reprendre au milieu :

```console
$ ./src/scripts/gate.sh --list
$ ./src/scripts/gate.sh check --from coverage
$ ./src/scripts/gate.sh check --only tidy
```

Une couverture qui casse à la trente-cinquième minute faisait repayer les
trente-quatre premières. Le `Makefile` passe de 472 à 287 lignes et redevient la
façade qu'il se dit être ; les cibles restent l'interface qu'on tape, et
`verify-gates.sh` les invoque toujours — c'est ce qui laisse ses preuves
intactes.

**Deux gardes**, parce que reprendre au milieu ouvre un mode d'échec qui
n'existait pas : un nom d'étape inconnu et une combinaison de filtres qui ne
retient rien font échouer l'invocation, plutôt que de rendre zéro sans avoir
rien fait.

## Ce qui a été lancé

| | État |
| :--- | :--- |
| `make check` | **vert**, 4 min 32 |
| `make check-local` | **vert**, 2 min 39 — relevé de banc versé sous `0.8.2`, charge 1,41, allure ×1,11 |
| `make verify-gates` | **vert**, 11 min 40 — **quarante-trois preuves**, dont les cinq nouvelles |

`verify-gates` passe de trente-neuf à quarante-trois : celle du périmètre
restreint disparaît avec le mécanisme qu'elle gardait, trois la remplacent — un
défaut dans une source, un dans un en-tête, une configuration durcie — et deux
couvrent les gardes de l'orchestrateur.

La CI garde `build/tidy` en cache d'Actions et ne passe plus de base : une pull
request et une exécution hebdomadaire lancent exactement la même commande.

Closes #269

author: matthijshart
body:
Paging through someone's photos felt inert, in both places it happens. Same root cause in each: **only one photo was ever mounted.**

`components/ui/PhotoViewer.tsx` and the carousel in `app/p/[uid]/page.tsx` both used `<AnimatePresence mode="popLayout">` with enter/exit variants. During a swipe you were dragging the current photo with *nothing beside it* — no neighbour to follow your finger — and on release it slid out while the next slid in from 100%.

That is a slide transition, not a carousel. It reads as unresponsive because nothing tracks the gesture.

Both are now **one continuous track**: every photo really is mounted side by side, positioned in pixels, so the neighbours move with the drag. `dragConstraints` span the real range, which gives 1:1 tracking through the middle and the iOS rubber-band at the first and last photo for free.

## Also fixed along the way

- **`dragElastic` was 0.25 in the viewer and 0.12 on the public page** — so even before the cross-fade problem, the photo moved a quarter (and an eighth) of the finger's travel. The track is dragged directly now.
- **The viewer used free 2D drag with `dragDirectionLock={false}`**, so a diagonal swipe half-paged and half-dismissed. It locks to one axis per gesture now, and swipe-down-to-dismiss no longer competes with paging.
- **Paging commits on distance (28% of a page) *or* flick velocity.** Previously a quick flick that travelled under 60px did nothing at all — which is exactly the gesture people make when they expect a photo carousel to be fast.
- **A cancelled swipe now explicitly springs back.** The settle effect only reacts to an index change, so without this the track would sit wherever the finger left it.
- **Track width is measured with a `ResizeObserver`**, so rotation and the iOS URL bar collapsing stay correct.

Dead state removed: the `direction` variable both components kept purely to choose an enter/exit direction.

## Verification

Production build passes, all 18 routes compile, `tsc` clean, `eslint` 0 errors.

**Not verified on a device.** This is entirely a feel change — the numbers (0.28 of a page, 400 velocity, spring 320/34) are reasoned defaults, not measured ones. One pass on a real phone will tell you whether paging wants to commit earlier or later.

## Summary
Fixes #2725. The FinOps → Utilization → "Database Sizes - Allocated vs Used" chart truncated the Allocated MB number on the left, reported on a wide screen in both fullscreen and windowed mode.

## Root cause
The size label (`"{Used} / {Total} MB"`) sat in a fixed `Width="90"` Grid column, right-aligned, with no wrapping or trimming. WPF clips a Grid cell's content to its arrange rect, so once the rendered text exceeded 90px — routine for any multi-hundred-GB database at 11.5pt font — the right-aligned text overflowed to the left and that overflow was silently clipped, cutting off the Allocated number's leading digits.

Both the Darling viewer (`Darling/PerformanceMonitor.Darling.Viewer/FinOpsTab.xaml`) and the Lite viewer (`Lite/Controls/FinOpsTab.xaml`) share identical markup for this chart, so both had the bug.

## Fix
Changed the column to `Width="Auto"` with `MinWidth="90"` in both viewers, so the column sizes to the actual text instead of clipping it.

author: kipergil
body:
Adds `/venues` — all nine halls on one map with their addresses — and the same map on each club page and venue page, **under** the address rather than in place of it. Every venue gets an **Open in Google Maps** button.

## The map

Leaflet with OpenStreetMap tiles. No API key, nothing to keep alive.

Three of this project's existing constraints ruled out the way a map is usually added to a React site, and each one shaped the implementation:

- **`script-src 'self'` has no exceptions**, so Leaflet is an npm dependency bundled and served from this origin, not the CDN script its own docs suggest.
- **Every page is prerendered with `renderToString`**, and Leaflet reaches for `document` as it initialises — importing it at module scope breaks the build for all 239 routes. It loads with a dynamic `import()` inside an effect, which also keeps ~150KB of mapping library in its own chunk, out of the initial bundle for the 237 pages with no map on them.
- **The map is never the only copy of the information.** Every page showing one also lists the venues in text with their addresses. The prerendered `/venues` carries all nine addresses as static HTML with no Leaflet in it, so the page works with JavaScript off, tiles blocked, or a screen reader on.

## Two things I got wrong, and caught by looking

**CARTO's basemaps are no longer key-free.** I built this first against Positron and Dark Matter, because they are a light/dark pair that would have matched the site's two themes. They render **watermarked "API KEY REQUIRED" across every tile**. Every request was HTTP 200; it only showed up in a screenshot. Esri's grey canvas comes back clean but splits labels into a second layer and its licensing for anonymous use is not something to guess at. So: OSM standard tiles — an explicit usage policy covering sites this size, labels in the tile, and it will still work in five years with nobody watching it.

**The bug that would have shipped.** The site sends `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`. OSM's tile servers answer a request carrying neither a Referer nor a recognised User-Agent with **HTTP 200 and a 7KB "Access blocked" image** in place of the map. Every map on the site would have been a wall of that notice, with no failed request, no console error and nothing in the logs — the same silent-success failure mode this project keeps hitting. Fixed with Leaflet's per-tile `referrerPolicy: "origin"`, where an element-level policy beats the document's: it sends the site's identity and none of the per-page detail `no-referrer` exists to withhold. The site-wide policy is untouched. There is a test on that single option, because deleting it breaks every map and nothing else notices.

## Geocoding

`npm run directus:geocode:venues` resolves each venue once via Nominatim and stores the result, so no page waits on a lookup from a car park with one bar of signal. All nine resolved. The script honours Nominatim's policy (identifying User-Agent, one request a second), skips venues that already have coordinates unless `--force` so a hand-corrected geocode outlives the next run, and **rejects any result outside the league's area** rather than storing it — a marker in Cumbria is worse than no marker, because no marker is visibly missing and a wrong one is not.

## Open in Google Maps

Uses coordinates rather than the venue name, because several of these halls share a name with a building in another county — "Village Hall, Furneux Pelham" is exactly the query a search answers confidently and wrongly. It falls back to the address for an ungeocoded venue and renders nothing at all when there is neither.

Every venue's stored `map_url` turned out to **already** be a name-based Google search, so that legacy link now renders only where it points somewhere Google is not. The same destination twice, and the weaker one, is not a choice. (`isGoogleMapsUrl` compares domain labels rather than substring-matching the host — the obvious regex calls `google.example.com` Google, which would let an attacker-chosen host suppress the real link. There is a test for that.)

## Incidental fix

The two copies of the CSP — helmet's for `/api/*`, `vercel.json`'s for pages — have carried a comment saying they are "meant to stay in step" since they were written, and nothing checked. Adding a tile host to both is what noticed. The shared directives are now exported and a test holds the two against each other. This is the same shape as the bug that took every deployment down for a day: config that is wrong in a way no test looks at.

Also updated the architecture note, which said "No Google Maps". What stays ruled out is the keyed embed/API; a link costs nothing but a URL, and the original note's suggested alternative — "a static map image" — turns out to need a key too.

## Accessibility

Markers are keyboard-focusable with the site's own focus ring; popups carry the venue name, club and address. Zoom controls are enlarged to the 48px target. Scroll-wheel zoom is off so the map does not hijack the page scroll on a phone. Animations respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Dark mode **dims** the tiles rather than inverting them — inversion produces a convincing dark map and destroys the place-name labels, which is the one thing a map of nine halls has to get right.

## Verification

- `tsc --noEmit` clean; **196 tests pass** (18 new, including the referrer-policy regression).
- `npm run build` prerenders **239 routes**; Leaflet lands in its own chunk (150KB JS + 15KB CSS), and `dist/public/venues/index.html` has all nine addresses and no `leaflet-container`, confirming it never ran server-side.
- Browser-checked `/venues`, `/clubs/hrc` and the venue page in light and dark: 9 pins, popups, 9 Google Maps links with correct coordinate hrefs, sticky attribution, no console errors.
- Reproduced the production `no-referrer` policy on the document and confirmed tiles still carry a Referer and return real imagery (34–55KB) rather than the 7KB block.

**One caveat.** This sandbox's browser has no outbound network, so I forwarded tile requests through Node — which does — carrying the browser's own headers. That is how both the CARTO watermark and the Referer behaviour were confirmed, but tiles have not been fetched by a browser talking to OSM directly. Worth a glance on the Vercel preview.

body:
## What

Runs the Squad 0.12.0 upgrade and records the two findings it produced.

## The upgrade itself is a no-op

The CLI is already at 0.12.0, the newest published version, and npm already resolves through `https://packagefeedproxy.microsoft.io/npm/` rather than the public registry, so there was nothing to fetch.

Measured effect of `squad upgrade` on this repo:

| Area | Result |
|------|--------|
| All 15 files in `.github/workflows/` | SHA-256 identical before and after |
| `.github/agents/squad.agent.md` | byte-identical to its own backup |
| ~70 files under `.squad/templates/` and `.github/skills/` | line-ending churn only, zero content change |
| `.github/skills/reviewer-protocol/SKILL.md` | **30 lines deleted, 0 added** |

The feared scaffolding resync did not happen. `squad-lead-gate.yml`, `squad-sync-dev.yml`, `squad-promote.yml` and `ci.yml` were untouched, so the branch protection work survived intact.

The single real change was a regression: the upgrade stripped the merge gate rules from `reviewer-protocol/SKILL.md`, including the section explaining why verdicts are PR comments under the shared `swigerb` identity. Nothing upstream replaced them. That deletion was reverted and the working tree is back to a clean state, so this PR carries no upgrade output at all.

## Why #283 actually went green

`team.md` credited the containment exemption. That is not what fired.

PR #283's own `CI`, `Squad CI` and `Squad Lead Gate` runs all ended `failure` with **zero jobs**, created 17:52:05Z and terminated 17:56:42Z, the exact second the PR merged. They were starved of runners and killed. Verified against a known-good run to rule out an API artifact.

What satisfied the ruleset was the SHA. A sync PR shares its head commit with `main`, so it inherits main's green check runs, and `squad-sync-dev.yml` publishes `Squad lead sign-off` directly against that SHA. Both the exemption and the self-published status reason from the same fact, that the commit is already on `main`, so neither widens what can merge.

## Changes

Documentation only, `.squad/team.md`:

- correct the sync explanation to match the measured behaviour
- note that starved duplicate runs are expected and are not a broken build
- add a **Squad upgrades** section recording the strip hazard and the `git diff --numstat` habit that catches it

## Verification

- `git diff --numstat` after restore: clean tree, no upgrade residue
- diff on this branch: `24 0 .squad/team.md`, additions only
- no em dashes in the added text

author: pepone
body:
Fixes #6644.

## The bug

With two relay nodes between two applications, several session creation exchanges are in flight at once — each
reconnection attempt can take a different route, and nothing serialized them. Neither node could tell one exchange
from another, so `SessionI::connected` committed whichever confirmation happened to arrive while the session was
disconnected, and silently dropped any that arrived while it was already connected.

Both CI occurrences are that, from opposite ends:

- **macOS** ([run 32167353565](https://github.com/zeroc-ice/ice/actions/runs/32167353565)) — the reply to a
  `confirmCreateSession` issued 28 ms and three attempts earlier arrived after the session had connected,
  disconnected and scheduled two retries, and was committed anyway. The relay's `disconnected` for that route had
  arrived 1 ms before and was dropped, because `disconnectedImpl` records nothing when the session is disconnected
  with a retry pending.
- **Windows** ([run 32051635716](https://github.com/zeroc-ice/ice/actions/runs/32051635716)) — two confirmations
  both got `Ok` (an intervening subscriber-side disconnect makes that possible), the publisher committed the one
  that arrived first and silently dropped the other, which was the one the subscriber had committed. The two sides
  ended up on different relay routes; one route died and only that side noticed.

Either way the nodes disagree permanently: the connected side answers every attempt with `AlreadyConnected`,
`checkSessionImpl` only probes the local relay connection which stays open, DataStorm never closes a connection
itself, and `destroyImpl` notifies nobody. The reader parks in `getNextUnread` / `getSessionConnection` until the
harness kills it.

## The fix

Each exchange carries an identifier. The subscriber allocates it, the publisher echoes it in
`confirmCreateSession`, and `Session::disconnected` names the exchange it refers to. Then:

- a session commits an exchange only while it is still the pending one;
- it ignores a disconnect notification for an exchange it has already replaced, so a route torn down after the
  session moved on cannot tear down its replacement;
- a creation request naming a *different* exchange is proof the peer no longer has this session, so the session is
  dropped and the new exchange takes over — instead of refusing the peer forever with `AlreadyConnected`;
- a new `SessionCreationError::Superseded` says "a newer exchange decides this", so the loser neither retries nor
  gives up.

## Wire compatibility

`createSession`, `confirmCreateSession` and `disconnected` change signature, and `SessionCreationError` gains an
enumerator. `Contract.ice` is internal — only `SampleEvent.ice` ships in `slice/`, and no other language mapping
implements the contract — so there is no public API impact, but DataStorm nodes running this build do not
interoperate with older ones. That is already true of 3.8.3: #6138 changed the lookup identity to
`DataStorm/Lookup2`, and `CHANGELOG-3.8.md` already tells users to upgrade all DataStorm nodes together.

## Testing

New `cpp/test/DataStorm/sessionHandshake` suite. The peer speaks the session protocol directly (its own minimal
restatement in `Test.ice`; it must not link libDataStorm, or the two copies of the generated contract compete to
supply the exception factories) and holds each `confirmCreateSession` response until the test releases it, so the
race is deterministic — no sleeps, no relays, no luck. It reproduced the macOS variant red before the fix
(`is ignoring 'createSession' ... already connected` ×100) and both halves of the fix are pinned by mutation.

- 14/14 DataStorm suites pass.
- `DataStorm/reliability` **30/30 clean** (16 topologies each, 480 topology runs), including both topologies named
  in the issue.
- Full C++ suite 110/111; `IceGrid/activation` fails only under `--workers=4` and passes standalone.
- macOS only so far — hence opening this for CI. The Windows variant is covered by the same commit rule but has no
  local repro.

author: osmanahmadxai
body:
Adds [Syncle](https://syncle.dev) to **Data Ingestion**, alongside entries like Airbyte, DBConvert Streams and Artie.

It moves rows between PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, SQLite, MongoDB and Redis in any combination. A bridge reads from a source table and writes to one or more destinations, fired one of three ways: a one-off backfill, a polling cursor, or change data capture read from the source's own change log — Postgres logical replication, MySQL binlog, MongoDB change streams, Redis keyspace notifications.

What distinguishes it from most of this section: there is no broker and no platform to stand up. It is four containers behind a single port with a web interface, aimed at one operator rather than a data team. Writes are idempotent upserts keyed by chosen columns, destination tables are created when missing with types translated across engines, and interrupted jobs resume from their cursor. HTTP endpoints work as a destination too.

Self-hosted, MIT licensed. Docs: https://syncle.dev/docs · Source: https://github.com/osmanahmadxai/SYNCLE

author: uda-lab-agent
body:
## Summary

[T26] Definition 3.2: "we regard `𝓧` as a subset of `C^∞(S¹)` with the relative topology" (after identifying `F` with `F|_{S¹}`). On `main`, `xRestrictS1 : AnalyticTestFn → TestFn` restricts an element of the analytic test-function class `𝓧` to its `S¹` boundary values, but `AnalyticTestFn` carried no topology. This PR encodes the sentence via a new module, `MobiusCPT/TestFunctions/AnalyticTopology.lean`.

**Encoded sentence:** "we regard `𝓧` as a subset of `C^∞(S¹)` with the relative topology" — the relative-topology half.

New declarations:
- `analyticTestFnTopologicalSpace : TopologicalSpace AnalyticTestFn := TopologicalSpace.induced xRestrictS1 inferInstance` — the relative topology, literally the pullback along the restriction map.
- `isInducing_xRestrictS1 : Topology.IsInducing xRestrictS1` (trivial, `⟨rfl⟩`).
- `continuous_xRestrictS1 : Continuous xRestrictS1`.
- `xRestrictS1_eq_iff (F G : AnalyticTestFn) : xRestrictS1 F = xRestrictS1 G ↔ Set.EqOn F.toFun G.toFun Oexterior`.

## Design history: the injectivity/embedding fork (see #53 for full record)

The original ruling on this Issue asked for `Function.Injective xRestrictS1` and `Topology.IsEmbedding xRestrictS1`. I found and proved this is **false**: `AnalyticTestFn.toFun : ℂ → ℂ` is a total function on `ℂ`, but none of the structure's five proof fields constrain its values strictly inside the open unit disc `{‖z‖ < 1}` (they reference only `Oexterior = {‖z‖ ≥ 1}`, `OexteriorInterior = {‖z‖ > 1}`, or behaviour at infinity). Two distinct `AnalyticTestFn` values can therefore agree everywhere on `Oexterior` (hence on the circle, hence have the same `xRestrictS1` image) while differing strictly inside the disc — an explicit counterexample is on the Issue.

Fable's amended ruling (2026-09-01, on #53) accepted the counterexample: the error was in the original ruling, not the landed encoding. `AnalyticTestFn` totalises the source's `𝓧` (a set of functions on `𝕆 = Oexterior` only) to all of `ℂ` as an encoding choice made at #7/#36; that totalisation makes literal injectivity of `xRestrictS1` on the raw type false, but the identification the source actually asserts — injective **on `𝕆`-data** — is exactly what `xRestrictS1_eq_iff` states. This PR does **not** claim `Topology.IsEmbedding xRestrictS1` or that the induced topology is `T0` on `AnalyticTestFn` anywhere. A quotient/partial-function redesign that would recover literal injectivity was explicitly ruled out of scope (would change every landed `AnalyticTestFn` statement for a property nothing downstream uses).

`xRestrictS1_eq_iff`'s forward direction is the pre-existing, unchanged `eqOn_Oexterior_of_xRestrictS1_eq`; the backward direction is new, using the pre-existing `xRestrictS1_apply`, `circle_subset_Oexterior`, and `TestFn.ext`. No existing declaration's statement or proof changed; `docs/` and `Contract.lean` untouched.

**Continuity statements this enables** (per the ruling's acceptance item): `xRestrictS1` continuity is the new content here. The density lemmas `lemma_3_4_density_upper/_lower` are statements about the image in `TestFn` and are unchanged by this PR; `Ṽ_τ`/`multiSmear` continuity statements live on `TestFn`/`strongTop` and are also unchanged.

## Validation

```
bash scripts/check.sh
```
Green: guards pass, `lake build` succeeds, live axiom audit OK (874 declarations ⊆ {propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound}), axiom-coverage guard OK (815 public theorems, all pinned). `analyticTestFnTopologicalSpace` is a data-valued (`TopologicalSpace`) instance, not `Prop`-valued, so per this project's established convention (compare `testFnTopologicalSpace` on `main`) it is correctly not pinned in `scripts/print_axioms.lean`; the three new `Prop`-valued theorems are.

## Review

- codex `adversarial-review` (`gpt-5.6-sol --effort high`, foreground): verdict **approve**, no material findings, after independently reading the amended-ruling history, the new file, and every pre-existing lemma it invokes, and confirming no `T0`/embedding claim was smuggled in.
- Internal review: read-only Sonnet subagent given the same numbered risks plus `git diff main...HEAD`: verdict **sound on all 7 risks**, no substantive findings; one style-only note (a dated process reference in the docstring) was applied as a follow-up commit.

Closes #53

author: monyrth
body:
Implements the ruling on ADR-0014's open question 2, accepted by rth on 2026-08-31: a member of a `Sodalitas` may name a dataset shared with that team as a run's input.

## What changed

`Datasets.findOwned` — the seam `CrystalApi._assertOwnedAditus` resolves a run's `owned: { genus: 'dataset' }` aditus reference through — takes the caller's team ids alongside the owner and admits a dataset whose `sodalitasId` is one of them. The query arms are `MongoDataset._page`'s, composed under `$and` for the same reason `_page` composes them that way.

The team ids are resolved **at dispatch**, from the authenticated caller, through the same `_callerTeamIds` helper the read path already uses, and are closed over in the lookup. Nothing about the caller's teams is attached to the `Actum` or threaded through execution — an `Actum` is identity-blind by design (ADR-0002), so the entry point is the whole of the gate. Membership is read live and never snapshotted, so it is a question re-answered on every run.

Everything else fails closed as before: no team store wired, an anonymous caller, or a dataset with no `sodalitasId` all fall through to owner-only. The refusal shape is unchanged — `input.invalid_aditus` naming only the port, so a caller still cannot tell "not yours" from "does not exist".

Scope: **datasets only**. The `owned: { genus: 'corpus' }` reference did not move (`Corpus` carries no team overlay), and the pre-written `access: 'public'` arms stay dark — public visibility is a separate ruling.

ADR-0014 records question 2 as ruled, with the consequence and what deliberately did not move.

## Note

`modus.aitoolkit-training` declares its `dataset` port as a **corpus** reference, so the ports this reaches today are the dataset-genus ones (`modus.dataset-caption`, `modus.dataset-decompose`) and any future modus declaring `owned: { genus: 'dataset' }`. Reconciling the two nouns is its own item; it is recorded as a follow-up on the ADR.

## Verify

- `npm run typecheck` — clean
- `npm run test:hermetic` — 2799 pass, 0 fail

New coverage in `tests/unit/allocutio/api/ownedResourceValidation.test.ts` (in the hermetic gate), where the declaration machinery is already pinned: a member dispatching against a shared dataset; a non-member refused with the refusal an unknown id already gives; a team-mate's unshared dataset staying owner-only; a dataset shared with a team the caller is not in refused; fail-closed with no team store and for an anonymous caller; no team identity on the dispatched `Inceptio`; losing membership closing the next dispatch while the run already dispatched is byte-for-byte unchanged and never re-resolved; and the corpus reference not widening. Five of these fail against the unfixed code; the closure cases pass in both directions, which is the point of them.

`tests/unit/crystal/MongoDataset.test.ts` pins the same predicate at the store (the `crystal-db` job — it needs a live Mongo).

author: charlesvestal
body:
Named module lists, with **Favorites** as a seeded default.

- **Module page** gains `Add to List`, showing how many lists hold this module.
- **Membership screen** toggles a mark per list and writes immediately.
- **Edit Lists / per-list actions** give Rename, Delete (confirmed) and Clear. Favorites offers Clear alone — the other rows are *absent*, not present-and-refusing.
- **Swap picker** gains a `List` row on top that cycles All → each eligible list → All, filtering the modules below. Lists are global, so a picker only offers lists holding an installed module of its own type.

Every rule lives in `src/shared/module_lists.mjs`, which imports nothing and takes its IO injected, so it is unit-tested under node (44 assertions). UI wiring is pinned by `test_module_lists_wiring.sh` (37) and additions to `test_trailing_pages_wiring.sh`. Every new assertion was mutated to prove it can fail.

### Things found along the way

- **`drawFooter` drops a hint pair that does not fit — silently, and every pair after it.** The membership screen asked for `JOG SEL, CLK TOGGLE, BACK MODULE` and rendered `JOG SEL … BACK MODULE`: the screen's primary action was the one word missing from its own footer. Found by rendering it and looking, not by reading it. Two related rules fell out of the same render — a footer names the verb of the row *under the cursor* (the filter row cycles and loads nothing), and a one-row screen must not name a JOG with nowhere to go.
- **Reopening the on-screen keyboard from inside its own `onConfirm` cannot work** — `text_entry.mjs` calls `closeTextEntry()` unconditionally after the callback, so a rejected duplicate name announced "Name in use" and then dropped both the keyboard and the text. Now deferred through the tick.
- **A failed write was announced as a success.** With an unreadable lists file every toggle flipped on screen, said "added", and persisted nothing. Same class as `move_midi_internal_send` returning true on a discarded write.
- **The test suite could not detect a missing draw case.** Deleting the ACTIONS case from the main render switch left everything green — the view would enter, announce, and draw nothing. That is the `PARAM_PAGES` war story one view over; the pin from `test_param_pages_wiring.sh` is now copied for all three new views.
- `drawChainPicker` was a second copy of the rectangle `chain_editor_chrome.mjs` exists to keep singular; it now delegates to the same `drawListScreen` the new screens use. Its 12 snapshot renders are byte-identical.

Screens were rendered and inspected via `tools/param-pages/preview_module_lists.mjs`. **Not yet run on hardware.**

author: neelamkhan123
body:
Adds a second deploy target alongside the on-demand AWS one: **any machine reachable over ssh**, the motivating case being an **Oracle Cloud Always Free VM** — 4 Ampere cores and 24 GB, free indefinitely. Same manifests, same k3s, but permanently live rather than created and destroyed per demo.

## Why

The AWS ephemeral path costs ~3p/hour and nothing in between, which is nearly free but not actually free, and it has no permanently-live URL. A host that is free *and* always on gives both. The trade is that the compute isn't AWS — the frontend, manifests, Kubernetes work and CI all stay exactly as they are.

## What's here

`deploy/remote-up.sh` (`task deploy:remote`) installs k3s if it isn't already there, then deploys. It creates no infrastructure and destroys none.

The manifest substitution and apply sequence **moved into `config.sh` as `ship_and_apply()`**, so both targets share one copy rather than drifting. The AWS path was regression-tested against the stub harness afterwards and behaves identically — same ConfigMap, same `COOKIE_SECURE` flip, same image substitution.

Two deliberate differences from the ephemeral path:

- **No certificate archiving.** A persistent host keeps Caddy's PersistentVolumeClaim across redeploys, so the Let's Encrypt rate-limit workaround the AWS path needs is unnecessary here.
- **An architecture guard.** The script compares the host's `uname -m` against what the images were built for and refuses to continue on a mismatch. Oracle's free shape is arm64; an amd64 image pulls perfectly and then dies with `exec format error`, which is a miserable thing to diagnose from inside a pod.

Images are now **multi-arch (arm64 + amd64)** by default, so one `:latest` runs anywhere. Both are pushed and verified.

## A real bug this surfaced

`bash -n` caught that an apostrophe inside `${VAR:?message}` is treated as an opening quote **even within double quotes**. It made the whole script unparseable, with the error reported about 60 lines from the actual cause. Worth knowing: the other `:?` usage in the codebase was checked and is clean.

## Testing

Stub harness again, since there's no host to deploy to yet:

| Scenario | Result |
|---|---|
| arm64 host, arm64 images, hostname set | deploys; ConfigMap gets the https URL and `COOKIE_SECURE: true`; k3s install attempted once |
| arm64 host, amd64-only images | **refuses**, naming the exact rebuild command |
| AWS path after the refactor | unchanged |

What this can't prove is a real deploy against a real VM — that needs the host to exist.

author: jcapona
body:
A visible sidebar with working agents measured **8.5% of one core** on a 20-session server. Profiling put almost none of it where I expected.

## What it wasn't

`animate_spinners` — the 4 Hz path — already writes only cursor-positioned glyph cells and costs **0.29ms**. My going-in hypothesis was that it redrew the tree each frame. It doesn't.

## What it was

Both hot functions were **flat with world size**: `collect()` cost the same at 5 sessions as at 30, and `render()` grew only 0.27ms per session on ~19.5ms of fixed cost. Fixed cost that ignores its input means forks, not work.

**Row padding.** `render()` padded every row with `$(printf '%*s' "$pad" '')`. `printf` is a builtin, but `$( )` forks a subshell regardless — **0.574ms vs 0.003ms** for `printf -v`. It runs once per rendered row, so the cost scaled with pane height rather than with anything visible.

**Platform check.** `$(uname)` picked between `stat -f` and `stat -c` at four sites, forking **3.2ms** to decide something that cannot change while the process runs. `$OSTYPE` is a shell variable at 0.02ms.

One of those four sites is in `cached_pane_status`, which the **switcher calls once per pane** — so this is switcher latency, not just background cost.

## Measured (20 sessions / 60 panes / 7 working)

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `render()` | 21.3 ms | **9.6 ms** |
| `collect()` | 11.9 ms | **10.7 ms** |
| per second | 3.39% | **2.10%** of one core |
| switcher, 65 panes | 437 ms | **280 ms** |

## Correctness

This is a pure refactor, so output must not move. A pinned-world render is **byte-identical** before and after, stable across three runs of each build.

Getting there took two corrections worth noting: the first comparison reported "identical" on two **0-byte** files — a vacuous pass — and the rebuilt one then showed a real diff (`zsh` vs `tmux`) that turned out to be a race in the fake world's `pane_current_command`, not the change. Pinning the panes to a fixed command made both builds deterministic.

`stat-portability.sh` asserts every `stat -f` sits inside a macOS guard by grepping for the literal `Darwin`, which `$OSTYPE == darwin*` does not contain. It now accepts either spelling, and still goes red when a guard is removed. Confirmed `$OSTYPE` is `linux-gnu` in the CI image, so the non-macOS branch still selects `stat -c`.

Suite is **44/44 on macOS and 44/44 on Linux**.

author: ibuilder
body:
# What & why

`ASSET-VERIFY`. `asset_rights.py` shipped both halves of a signed release manifest and **only sealing was reachable**. Counted against `services/api/src`, `services/data/src` and `apps/web/src`, excluding the module itself:

| function | production callers |
|---|---|
| `verify_release` · `verify_signature` · `verify_content_hash` · `verify_manifest_hash` | **0** |
| `public_key_b64` · `generate_seed` | **0** |
| `sign_manifest` · `build_manifest` · `new_asset_id` | 1 each |

A manifest exists so that *someone else* can confirm a release is authentic and unaltered. Sealing alone produces a file nobody can check — including us.

* **`POST /asset-rights/verify`** takes the `asset_rights.json` out of a `.mass` and reports findings separately — `content_hash_ok`, `manifest_hash_ok`, `signed`, `signature_ok`, `trusted_key` — because *"the content was altered"* and *"it carries no signature"* call for different responses.
* **`GET /asset-rights/status` now serves `public_key`.** Its docstring said *"never the key itself"*, which read as a rule against publishing **any** key. The public half is what verifiers need, and the same key is already embedded in every signed manifest we emit — withholding it protected nothing and left a recipient trusting the document's own copy, which is the copy an attacker would have replaced.
* **`python -m aec_api.asset_rights --generate`** mints a signing seed. Without it the *signed* path was unreachable from a clean deployment except by generating an Ed25519 key out of band. A command and deliberately **not** a route: minting a private key is an operator action at the machine.

## The design error, caught by writing the test rather than reading the code

The plan was to default `public_key` to this deployment's key "so `trusted_key` means something". That is backwards, and the test's trust matrix is what showed it:

| supplied key | `signature_ok` | `trusted_key` |
|---|---|---|
| none — falls back to the key **in the document** | true | **false** |
| the right trusted key | true | **true** |
| a *different* key | **false** | false |

A release signed by anyone else would land in that third row — reported as a **bad signature** when it is perfectly valid. The key is the caller's to supply.

## A client method was written and then deleted

`verifyRelease()` had nothing in the UI calling it, so it would have been an **unwired client method added to make a reachability gate go green** — the exact defect this release removes, introduced while removing it. The party who verifies a release is whoever received the file, with their own tooling, like `/auth/cloud/callback`.

## A blind spot recorded rather than worked around

The reachability gate **cannot see the new route in either direction**: the leaf `verify` occurs in 25 unrelated web files, so the substring rule reads it as called — and for the same reason it cannot be frozen as uncalled. author: hussainmansoor876
body:
## Problem

The `/search` page is rendered entirely by `validateSearch()` in `app.js`, which only queried the store API with `title=<q>`. Products whose product code lives in the slug/SKU rather than the title (BK461-ORG, BK461-LM, BK461-BLK — e.g. `/safety-products-catalog/BK461-ORG`) therefore never came back and the page showed "Nothing found".

Two further bugs in the same function:

- Pagination advanced `skip` by the requested `limit` (50) even when the API returned fewer items, silently skipping whole pages; with an empty page and a non-zero `totalCount` the loop never terminated.
- The query was sent to the API unencoded, and an empty `q` still fired a `title=null` request.

## Changes

- Products are now matched against their code fields as well as the title. The API call and a full catalogue fetch run in parallel; the catalogue is filtered locally on `title`, `url`/slug, `sku`, `code`, `model`, `brand`, tags, categories and every variant SKU. Both result sets are merged and de-duplicated, so nothing that was found before is lost. `bk461`, `BK461-ORG` and `bk461org` all match.
- Results are ranked: exact code/title matches first, then prefix matches.
- Pagination advances by the number of items actually returned, with a page guard.
- The query is URL-encoded, and an empty query skips the request entirely.
- The `q` parameter is HTML-escaped before being echoed back into the search input — previously `?q=">``<img src=x onerror=...>'`` gave reflected XSS.

## Testing

Matching and pagination helpers were exercised against mock data in Node (code matches, partial codes, condensed codes, multi-word queries, empty queries, short pages), and `node --check app.js` passes. The live API was not reachable from the dev environment, so please verify `https://shop.bigkclothing.ca/search?q=BK461-ORG` (plus `BK461`, `BK461-LM`, `BK461-BLK`) once this is merged and GitHub Pages has served the new `app.js`.

author: emmymay
body:
## Outcome

Add the server-side foundation for retained room work evidence: one stable snapshot per canonical room, source message, and durable agent identity. This is a secondary host report, never execution, delivery, liveness, or approval authority.

## Scope

- Strict version-1 public summary: fixed recorded-state values, bounded operation outcome counts, elapsed time, and incomplete-evidence marker. Unknown fields are rejected. No free-form strings, command text, output, paths, native handles, or credentials are accepted.
- Separate PostgreSQL snapshot table with immutable owner/host/installation/agent-instance custody. Source/owner deletion cascades. No existing receipt or artifact model is repurposed.
- Host-only POST `/supervisor-host-grants/:grantId/worker-sessions/:sessionId/agent-work`, under the existing grant rollout flag and exact route allowlist. Reuses current grant/repository access validation; no owner/worker bearer fallback.
- GET `/rooms/:roomId/agent-work` (latest 50 visible snapshots, truthful truncation) and `/rooms/:roomId/agent-work/:attemptId`, for authenticated human room participants. Source visibility is filtered before limiting; concealed/missing detail has the same 404. Responses do not disclose publisher custody, grant/session IDs, or digests.

## Write invariants

The write transaction locks/revalidates the grant row, exact captured/selected worker sessions in sorted order, the source message, then the source receipt. This order preserves retirement and source-pruning lock order. Reprovision token rotation is fenced even though that older path does not take the grant advisory lock.

An active captured session remains the exact publisher. Once it ends, admission requires one unique same-owner live successor, rechecked after the receipt lock. This is an admission-time rule, not an exclusive lifetime claim. The immutable publisher tuple rejects implicit cross-host or cross-instance takeover.

Revision is publisher-owned and independent of grant generation. Equal revision + equal canonical digest is idempotent; lower revision or equal revision with changed content is a persistent conflict response with the stored snapshot unchanged. Grant handoff or normal session renewal does not mint another public attempt. A future publisher must durably retain its revision and must not resolve conflicts by blindly incrementing stale data.

## Deliberate limits / non-goals

- Owner-scoped grants and non-rental sources only. This does not expand rental visibility or worker API capabilities.
- Ended workers cannot upload. A final-shutdown tail produced after session retirement remains local-only; the eventual publisher must flush during work rather than rely on a death-time flush. Existing stored evidence remains readable after retirement.
- No polling/cursor format, events, daemon publisher, retention sweep, UI, approval/delegation, or authority/default/profile changes. Concealment-safe polling and publication/retention are subsequent slices; no publisher is enabled before those are ready.
- No release, npm version bump, runtime pin, or rollout activation.

Fable approved this bounded write + on-demand GET split and the recovery limits in the Focus room (messages 428–431).

## Verification

- Staging baseline supervisor integration suite: 33/33.
- `TEST_DB_URL=postgresql://letagents_test@127.0.0.1:55489/agent_work_tests_utf8 node --import tsx --test src/api/__tests__/supervisor-host-grant-integration.test.ts`: 41/41 against a private temporary PostgreSQL instance; every test migrates a fresh schema.
- `node --import tsx --test src/api/request/__tests__/supervisor-grant-route-registry.test.ts src/api/__tests__/message-info-read-receipts.test.ts`: 23/23.
- `npx tsc --noEmit`: passed.
- `git diff --check`: passed.

New coverage protects strict summary admission; credential/membership boundaries; alias resolution; concealed detail/list behavior; concurrent conflicting revisions; stable identity across renewal/handoff/successor recovery; explicit cross-host/instance refusal; final-shutdown refusal; source cascades; and grant-rotation/source-deletion races on real database connections.

Independent storage review caught the source/receipt lock-order cycle, corrected before PR submission. Dalton independently approved the full 11-file slice and reran all 41 integration tests and TypeScript successfully. His final coverage suggestion (a real foreign-owner same-key worker, rather than only a missing session) is now covered by the successor regression. Fable review and exact-head CI remain required before squash merge into staging.

author: petersalomonsen
body:
The last of the `conversation too large` failures — and the only one that wasn't waste.

#207 removed the echoed reasoning. #213 removed stale copies of documents the model had re-read. And a session **still** arrived at 60,892 chars against the proxy's 60k cap, across 84 messages of genuine work with nothing left to squeeze.

Pruning buys a fixed slice. Only compaction bounds a session.

## What it does

The client compacts **before** a turn once the conversation passes **42,000 chars** — 70% of the cap. Before, not after: the proxy refuses an oversized conversation outright, so reaching the cap mid-turn loses that turn rather than degrading gracefully.

## Summarise, not truncate

Dropping the oldest turns is cheaper and needs no model call. It also severs `tool_calls` from their results and throws away the decisions that explain the current state.

In this app the **documents carry the work** and the **conversation carries why**. So the summary asks for what was built and where it lives, what the user corrected, and *what they changed by hand* — exactly what a later turn needs, and exactly what a truncation destroys.

The summary returns as a **user** turn. A history that opens with the assistant asserting things it cannot see is a worse starting point than one where it's told them.

A failed compaction doesn't take the turn with it — the conversation is long, not broken, and the turn may still fit. It says so and carries on.

This mirrors what the SDK path has always done at its own threshold, so both providers now behave the same way instead of one silently having no answer.

## Tests

Unit: the whole history goes into the summary request, a short one comes back, the system prompt survives, and the threshold sits below the proxy cap but not so low it discards context that still fits.

E2E: a reply large enough to cross the threshold, then a second message — asserting the chat shows `compacting the conversation`, that `Summarise this session` actually reached the API, and that the turn carried on afterwards.

81 agent-tools, 139 gitproxy, 5/5 nearai e2e, 11 Playwright across nearai + paywall.

body:
## What
Upgrades `ngrok-api-go` from v7 to v9, and uses ngrok's [API filtering](https://ngrok.com/docs/api/api-filtering) to look up reserved domains by hostname.

## How
- Bump the dependency to v9. `List()` on resources that support CEL filtering now takes `*ngrok.FilteredPaging`, so `ngrokapi.Lister` is split into `Lister` and `FilteredLister`, and the shared mock base client is generic over the paging type.
- v9 switches JSON tags from `omitempty` to `omitzero`, so a non-nil empty slice is serialized instead of dropped. Guard the few call sites that could send one on a KubernetesOperator or CloudEndpoint create/update, so behavior is unchanged.
- Regenerate the BoundEndpoint CRD. `ngrok.Ref` is inlined into `status.endpoints[]`, and since its fields now use `omitzero`, controller-gen marks `id` and `uri` as required. The operator always populates both from the ngrok API, so what it writes is unchanged.
- `findReservedDomainByHostname` now filters on an exact hostname match server-side, instead of paging through every reserved domain on the account and filtering client-side.

## Breaking Changes
None for users. The only schema change is the required `id`/`uri` noted above, on operator-owned status fields.

author: rodrigorom2105
body:
## Problem

No Supabase client was parameterised with a `Database` type, so every `.from()`, `.rpc()`, `insert()` and `update()` in the app resolved to `any`. Column names, nullability and payload shapes went unchecked all the way to the wire.

## Change

Generate `src/lib/supabase/database.types.ts` from the remote project and pass it to all four clients (browser, server, proxy, service role). Row shapes in `src/types/index.ts` now derive from it instead of being hand-written copies.

## Drift the typing surfaced

The hand-written types had already fallen behind the schema:

- **`Query` was missing `prompt_tokens`, `completion_tokens` and `embedding_tokens`** — the three columns added by the recent token-metering work (#5).
- **`Document` was missing `embedding_tokens`.**
- **`queries.tokens_used` and `queries.document_id` are nullable** but were declared non-null. `query-history` compared a possible `NULL` with `> 0`.
- **`User` described a `public.users` table that does not exist** — users live in `auth.users`. It had no callers; removed.
- **The ask page listed its columns by hand and had missed `embedding_tokens`**, so the row it passed on was not a full `Document`. It wants `select('*')`.

## pgvector on the wire

PostgREST exposes `vector` as text, so embeddings now go out as `JSON.stringify(embedding)`. This is the same bytes on the wire — Postgres parses `[0.1,0.2]` as a vector literal whether the JSON holds an array or the equivalent string.

Verified against the live project rather than assumed:

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `match_document_chunks` with vector as JSON string | `200` |
| `match_document_chunks` with vector as JSON array (old path) | `200` |
| Control: malformed vector | `400 22P02` — so the cast really happens |
| Insert with dangling `document_id`, both forms | identical `409 23503` FK rejection, nothing written |

## Regenerating

`pnpm db:types` regenerates the file. Because there is no baseline migration, it reads the remote project, not `supabase/migrations/`. **Run it in the same commit as any migration**, or the committed types drift silently.

## Left out on purpose

`documents.status` is plain `text` with no constraint, so its generated type is `string`. `DocumentStatus` is kept as an app-level union over what we *write*; it is not a promise about what the database returns. Pushing the union into the generated type needs a real Postgres enum — a migration on a table with data, so not done here.

## Verification

`pnpm type-check` and `pnpm build` pass. `pnpm lint` was already failing on `main` (10 errors / 16 problems); this branch is at 9 / 15 — no new failures, and one `any` removed (`storeTempData` now takes `Json`). The remaining errors are pre-existing and unrelated.
