author: musharna
body:
## What

First lens-distortion dogfood on the real PlantCV fisheye tutorial photo (`fisheye_test_img.jpg` + `checkerboard_imgdir`, plantcv tests/testdata — used from tmp, not vendored). The released 1.7.0 pipeline was run on the distorted photo and on the same photo undistorted through PlantCV's own checkerboard calibration; the deltas are the evidence for every change here.

**Measured:** distortion inflates the centre-frame plant's area **2.13x** (width 1.69x, height 1.22x), shifts shape traits (eccentricity 0.56 → 0.76, ellipse angle 34° → 11°), and gives the same physical pot three different pixel scales — rim width **1.728x**, face height **1.313x**, base width **1.591x**. The error is anisotropic: a px_per_mm calibrated on the rim mis-sizes area by −29%, one on the face height by +24%. No scalar compensates.

## Changes

1. **`correct_lens_distortion`** — the fourteenth tool, and the first that writes (annotated `read_only_hint: false`). Checkerboard dir → calibration (cached on the directory's content digest) → `<image>_undistorted.png` next to the input, cropped to the valid-pixel ROI so the remap's fabricated black voids are not left for a value threshold to measure (on the real photo the voids were 58% of the frame). Reports what `pcv.transform.checkerboard_calib` discards: frames used/skipped **by name**, rms reprojection error. <3 detectable boards → typed `LensCalibrationError` (PlantCV crashes with a raw cv2 error on 0 frames and "calibrates" from 1 without comment). An explicit `output_path` refuses to overwrite an existing file; the derived name is the tool's own. Advisories: `lens_corrected`, `thin_calibration` (<5 frames), `distortion_voids_remain`.
2. **`minor_components_inflate_extent`** (every segmenter + measurer): on the real photo, a 1,818-px sliver at (2824, 0) — 0.4% of the 458k-px plant — made `measure()` report width **2040 px (true 940)**, corrupt longest_path/ellipse/convex-hull, with `warnings: []` (multi_specimen needs a major object, frame_clipping deliberately ignores minor slivers since 1.6.0, noisy needs dozens). Fires when non-major components stretch the union extent >10% beyond the MAJOR components' own union — so a genuine second plant (multi_specimen territory) does not trip it; names the offender and the `keep_largest`/`fill_size` remedy.
3. **`marker_touches_crop_edge`** now also names the no-isolatable-marker case: the pot+soil+plant is ONE contiguous dark object, four plausible pot crops returned px_per_mm 10.8–18.1, and the old message only suspected polarity.

Docs: GUIDE gains a "Correcting lens distortion" section with the measured numbers, the warning table gains the four new codes, the refusals paragraph gains `LensCalibrationError`; README tool table + code count (the "26" was already stale — 33 now); INSTRUCTIONS point at the tool.

## Tests

335 (16 new, every one watched RED first — the three lens-impl tests failed on the missing module/impl, the advisory tests on the exact empty-warnings gap, the message test on the missing sentence). Lens ground truth is synthetic: fixed-pose checkerboard views distorted through a known camera model; "corrected" is asserted as corner rows becoming collinear again (4.4 px bend → <50%), with positive controls inside the refusal tests. Real-execution check: the tool run against the 9 real checkerboard photos + real fisheye image through live code (9 used, `bad_checkerboard.png` skipped by name, corrected image re-segments to a single clean component), and the new advisory fires on the real photo at segment and measure.

## Release

Version bumped to 1.8.0 (pyproject, server.json, CITATION.cff); CHANGELOG entry added. PyPI upload precedes tag push as usual.

body:
Infrastructure updates currently stop `remote.futrx.service` while project containers are recycled. That also removes the only API serving update status, so the Settings page freezes on its last log line for the longest part of the update and makes healthy work look stuck.

This PR keeps the control plane online during workspace recycling. The upgrader publishes a live-PID maintenance marker, and the prompt service rejects new interactive and scheduled runs while that marker is active. Existing agent runs remain protected by the upgrader's existing busy-workspace skip behavior. The marker is removed on success or failure, and stale or orphaned markers fail open.

Update phases and per-workspace progress are written atomically to durable state. The admin update API now returns the current phase, completed/total workspace counts, current workspace, progress timestamp, ANSI-clean log output, and the log modification time. Settings renders that data as a progress panel and clearly explains brief application reconnects.

author: brettluelling
body:
Closes REQ-605.

`ci.yml` kept one in-flight run per ref and cancelled the older one, so pushing
commit *n+1* killed commit *n*'s run — almost always inside
`fmt · clippy · test (macos-latest)`, the slowest of the seven job runs and the
runner that caught LESSON-591's race. REQ-599 lost that leg on two of its seven
commits. REQ-600 kept it only by pushing one commit at a time and waiting.

**The change is one line.**

```diff
-  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
+  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}-${{ github.sha }}
```

`cancel-in-progress` stays `true` — with the SHA in the group it still collapses
duplicate runs of the *same* commit (a re-run, a close/reopen), which is the only
kind of superseding GitHub's concurrency primitive can actually recognise.

## OQ-1, settled (ADR-1)

- **Dropping `cancel-in-progress`** was rejected as the *worst* option, not the
  simplest: `false` does not mean "run both", it means **queue**. Every commit
  would still serialize — the exact wall-clock cost REQ-600 paid by hand — and it
  is the only candidate that creates the queue AC-3 worries about.
- **Gating on event type** was rejected on evidence: `main`'s push runs have the
  same defect (run `33445087015`, cancelled at 219s), and AC-1's "one branch"
  includes `main`.
- `github.sha` rather than `github.event.pull_request.head.sha`: one expression
  covers both triggers, and uniqueness per tree under test is the only property
  the key needs — which the merge SHA has as well as the head SHA, so the choice
  does not depend on resolving which one `github.sha` is.

## AC-1 — demonstrated, not assumed

Six commits pushed one at a time, each while the previous run was still in
flight (status **verified** before each push, not inferred from timing). Every
consecutive pair overlapped, so no observation is vacuous.

| # | run | commit | config | conclusion |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | 33450647558 | `3c664a8` | old | **cancelled** |
| R2 | 33450729742 | `ebe6841` | old | success |
| R3 | 33450814843 | `5b5af36` | **new** | success |
| R4 | 33450882606 | `8cbdb7c` | **new** | success |
| R5 | 33451033687 | `a165c72` | **new** | success |

- **Before** (R1→R2, both old, 19s overlap): R1 died with the macOS leg running.
  It took *both* `check` legs this time.
- **Mixed** (R2→R3, old→new): recorded and **excluded** — different groups, so
  they could not have collided under either setting. Not evidence for either half.
- **After** (R3→R4, 153s overlap; R4→R5, 65s overlap): both survived and passed.
  R3 was still running when **both** R4 and R5 started.

## AC-2 — measured, with the rule beside the count

**Rule R** = per job `ceil(sec/60)`, summed. **Rule W** = Rule R with GitHub's OS
multipliers (ubuntu ×1, macOS ×10) — a resource-intensity proxy, *not* an invoice:
this repo is public and GitHub bills none of it. (`timing.billable` returns
`total_ms: 0` here, so job timestamps are the source.)

The finding that makes the trade easy: **a cancelled run costs almost what a
completed one costs.** In 4 of 4 cancelled runs the kill lands inside `Tests`,
*after* toolchain install, cache restore, formatting and clippy have all
succeeded — returning ~10s of macOS time, destroying the whole macOS result, and
skipping `Post Cache cargo build` so the next run starts colder.

For a 7-commit PR:

| | Rule R | Rule W | commits with macOS evidence |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Before-A — push freely (REQ-599) | 82.2 | 379 | 1 of 7 |
| Before-B — wait for each (REQ-600) | 84.0 | 399 | 7 of 7 |
| **After** | **84.0** | **399** | **7 of 7** |

**+2% against Before-A** for six macOS results that did not exist; **exactly
nothing against Before-B**, and it hands back the wall-clock (REQ-600: 10 runs
across 2h01m for 34m of run time).

## AC-3 — the trade, named

**Given up:** cancellation of a *superseded* commit's run — a force-push
abandoning X leaves X's run to finish on a tree nobody merges.
**Gained:** every tip keeps a complete result on every runner.
**Why not both:** `concurrency` keys on a string with no notion of ancestry, so
it cannot tell "n+1 builds on n" from "Y replaces X".
**Why bounded, not indefinite:** an abandoned run finishes its own jobs and
stops; distinct-SHA groups never queue behind one another, so nothing
accumulates. The failure mode AC-3 names is unreachable here — and *reachable*
under `cancel-in-progress: false`.

## Beyond the one line

`release.yml` and `deploy-site.yml` both explained themselves with "**Unlike
ci.yml**, an in-flight run is NOT cancelled by a newer one". Both sentences go
false on the commit that lands this, and nothing in the linter or the suite would
ever have caught it (LESSON-599). Both are rewritten to the new contrast — those
two **queue**; `ci.yml` runs distinct commits **concurrently** — each keeping its
own reason for `false`. Comment-only: neither diff contains a non-comment line.
Three other `ci.yml` references were checked and are unaffected.

Three risks the diff did not name are recorded in the architecture doc: cargo-cache
contention (checked, and the check was **weak** — the concurrent runs touched no
Rust code so no save was attempted, and it could not have revealed a collision);
the incidental per-PR rate limit the old group provided, now gone; and that the
property has no automated guard, with the reasoning for leaving it that way.

## AC-4

`actionlint 1.7.12` — `ci.yml`'s own pinned version — shellcheck-backed, `rc=0`,
run exactly as the `tooling` job runs it. Clean on the baseline before any edit
and after both workflow commits. No job name, trigger, or matrix entry changed,
so all six required status checks still report.

```adlc-footprint
teton-code:.adlc/specs/REQ-605-ci-concurrency-per-commit/requirement.md
teton-code:.github/workflows/ci.yml
teton-code:.github/workflows/deploy-site.yml
teton-code:.github/workflows/release.yml
```

author: losakovvitalik
body:
## Summary

Since #154, sending the GitHub token to a repository URL was a two-part obligation: canonicalise the URL with `canonicalRepoUrl`, then build the header env with `authEnv`. Three call sites in `apps/desktop/src/main/git.ts` paired the two by hand; a fourth that built the env but handed git the raw URL would send the `Authorization` header to `www.github.com`, fail on the refused redirect (redirects are off per #135/#143), and be misreported by the #154 error mapping as "the repository has moved".

- New `githubTarget(url, token): { target, env }` returns the pair, so the URL git receives and the URL the header was authorised for cannot diverge.
- `listRemoteBranches`, `cloneRepo` and `cloneAuthEnv` go through it; `canonicalRepoUrl` and `authEnv` have no other callers left, so no call site can build the env for a URL it did not canonicalise.
- The 3xx branch in the git runner no longer infers "this call ran with redirects disabled" from the truthiness of `env` (a proxy an unrelated future env would silently break): `redirectsDisabled(env)` reads the `http.followRedirects=false` pair off the env itself — the fact the moved-repository explanation actually depends on.

Refactor only: no user-facing change, and no change to which hosts receive the token. The host allowlist from #135/#143 is untouched — the token is attached only for `github.com` / `www.github.com`, lookalike hosts still fail closed, and the existing `git.test.ts` suite keeps proving it (allowlist, lookalikes, `www.` repoint on update, and both sides of the moved-repository mapping all pass unchanged).

Closes #155

## Testing

- `cd apps/desktop && pnpm run typecheck` — passes (`tsc --noEmit` on both `tsconfig.node.json` and `tsconfig.web.json`).
- `cd apps/desktop && pnpm test` — 16 files, 132 tests passed, including all 26 in `git.test.ts` (token allowlist, lookalike hosts, `www.github.com` canonicalisation/repoint, moved-repository mapping with and without auth).

against the spread of each cell's five timed repeats, 18 of 20 cells agree
within twice that spread. The largest absolute residual, 9.2 ms at
`iid_gaussian` d=2048 N=128, sits on a cell whose own repeats span 10.5 ms.
The previous text treated that residual as an unexplained term bounding the
model's precision; most of it was never there to explain.

**Two cells do exceed it**, both `iid_gaussian` at d=512: N=256 at 2.5x its
spread and N=1024 at 7.7x. Both positive, so A is slower in a real generation
than the isolated contraction accounts for. `iid_gaussian` is the only arm
that materializes the population, so the leading candidate is that A's
replicated contraction runs while `ask`'s materialized population is still
resident and competes for bandwidth, which the isolation harness cannot see.

`contraction_isolation.py --resident` allocates a population-sized buffer
before timing, which is the test. `sweep-iid512-recheck.yaml` is the config
for it, committed unrun. Two cells is a thin basis for a rental, so this is
here as a named question rather than a pending campaign.

Conflict resolution worth a look: the paragraph in Section 6 conflicted with
main's v5e decomposition text. The branch's version asserted the v5e
decomposition was not run, which main has since disproved, so the merged
paragraph keeps the repeat-noise finding and main's v5e result and drops that
clause. The same staleness appeared inside the results README, where the
rebase put "the v5e is not measured" above the v5e section itself; that
paragraph now scopes the residual analysis to the A100 instead.

Paper builds clean, 27 pages, no undefined references.

author: achubaty
body:
Repoints `install-spatial-deps` from `50d9a4d2b92e363a902fb98fee4f4a6f6d0938af ` to `@main` — **1** reference(s) in `.github/workflows/update-citation-cff.yaml `.

### Why

Every published tag of that action — v0.1 through v0.5, **including the newest** — still runs:

```
add-apt-repository -y ppa:ubuntugis/ubuntugis-unstable
```

That PPA installs **libgdal37** (GDAL 3.11.x). Posit's noble binary cache builds sf/terra against the Ubuntu-default **libgdal34** — confirmed by `objdump` on the PPM noble tarballs, which need `libgdal.so.34`, `libproj.so.25`, `libgeos_c.so.1`. The mismatch surfaces only at lazy-load, as `libgdal.so.34: cannot open shared object file`, and takes the whole job with it.

Only `@main` dropped the PPA (PredictiveEcology/actions#25). Tags do not move, so pinning to one keeps the hazard — which is why "pin to the newest tag" is currently the wrong advice for this action.

This repo's own history records the failure in both directions: a cached terra built against one libgdal while the runner supplied the other. The underlying cause was a stale `setup-r-dependencies` package cache outliving a change in the runner's system GDAL — the PPA is what made the two disagree.

### Note

On the pak path this step is largely redundant anyway: `setup-r-dependencies` → `pak::lockfile_install()` → `install_sysreqs()` already installs `libgdal-dev`, `gdal-bin`, `libgeos-dev`, `libproj-dev`, `libsqlite3-dev` and `libudunits2-dev` from stock noble apt, and pak's own rules add the ubuntugis PPA only for Ubuntu 14.04/16.04. Removing the step entirely is a separate change, gated on a self-test run — this PR only makes the pin correct.

author: shenjun93
body:
## Root cause

Real Starlette qualification runs exposed two nested-runtime gaps:

- Codex platform packages include `codex-code-mode-host`, but Qualock only mounted the main `codex` binary.
- Codex Linux workspace sandbox requires bubblewrap plus user-namespace syscalls that Docker's default seccomp profile blocks.

## Fix

- Resolve and fingerprint `codex-code-mode-host` alongside the main binary.
- Mount support binaries read-only into the agent container.
- Treat structured Codex `item.completed(type=error)` events as agent errors.
- Bake pinned `bubblewrap=0.8.0-2+deb12u1` into prepared Debian runtime images.
- Relax seccomp only for the agent container (`seccomp=unconfined`) so inner bubblewrap can create its namespace. No `--privileged`, `SYS_ADMIN`, or AppArmor disable is used. Grader containers keep Docker's default seccomp profile.

## TDD / verification

- Initial focused RED: 3 failures for missing support binary contract, error-event parsing, and support-binary mount.
- Bubblewrap Dockerfile RED confirmed runtime prerequisite was absent.
- Seccomp RED confirmed agent container lacked the minimal namespace allowance.
- Final local suite: 88 passed.
- Direct Docker probes: default seccomp blocks `unshare -Ur` and bwrap; `seccomp=unconfined` alone makes both pass.
- Live production-style Starlette / Codex 0.150.0 / GPT-5.6 Terra smoke: `valid=true`, hidden grader PASS, duration 88.4s. This is the first end-to-end successful agent→commands→patch→freeze→hidden-grader run.

author: mateo-berri
body:
## TLDR

Problem this solves:

- Errors on `/v1/messages` came back in OpenAI's error envelope
- `type` and `param` were the literal string `"None"`
- Anthropic-format clients expect `{"type":"error","error":{...}}` per Anthropic's docs

How it solves it:

- The route now returns Anthropic's documented error envelope for every error it handles
- Error type is mapped from the status code (400 -> `invalid_request_error`, 429 -> `rate_limit_error`, ...)
- Guardrail detail from dict-detail blocks still rides along under `error.provider_specific_fields`
- `request_id` echoes the client's `x-request-id`, matching the existing context-management error path
- Response headers (`x-litellm-call-id`, ...) and OTel server-span error stamping are preserved

## User Flow

Before: a developer whose Anthropic-format app hits a guardrail block gets an OpenAI-shaped error with `"None"` strings, so their Anthropic error handling can't classify it

1. Their app sends POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages with `{"model": "claude-sonnet-5", "messages": [...]}` and the message trips the admin's content guardrail
2. The response is HTTP 400 with `{"error": {"message": "Content blocked: keyword 'kumquat' detected", "type": "None", "param": "None", "code": "400"}}`
3. That is OpenAI's envelope, not the `{"type": "error", "error": {"type": ..., "message": ...}}` shape api.anthropic.com returns, and the error type reads as the string `"None"`
4. Their error handling, written against Anthropic's documented format, finds no `type: "error"` marker and no usable error type, so the block surfaces as an unclassified failure

After: the same request comes back exactly in Anthropic's documented error format

1. Their app sends the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages and the message trips the same guardrail
2. The response is HTTP 400 with `{"type": "error", "error": {"type": "invalid_request_error", "message": "Content blocked: keyword 'kumquat' detected", "provider_specific_fields": {...}}, "request_id": "req-..."}`
3. That matches what api.anthropic.com itself returns for a 400, so their Anthropic error handling classifies it like any other invalid-request error, and the guardrail detail is still there under `error.provider_specific_fields`

Resolves LIT-6468

Shared setup: proxy run from the worktree with `python litellm/proxy/proxy_cli.py --config config.yaml --port <port>` (before leg on 35768 at the merge base, after leg on 20535 at this PR's tip), real Anthropic API key, master key `sk-1234`

author: chrismichaelps
body:
Closes #174. Implements [[ADR-0014 Parameters of Higher Kind]].

`map` was written five times — `Array`, `Option`, `Result`, `Iter`, `Tree` — and
the five could not be related. A trait could not say `F[A] -> F[B]`, because a
parameter stood for a *type* and applying one was refused. No function could
take "some container" and transform what it held.

```pudu
trait Mappable[F[_]] {
  fn mapped[A, B](self: &F[A], transform: fn(A) -> B) -> F[B]
}

export fn over[F[_]: Mappable, A, B](values: &F[A], transform: fn(A) -> B) -> F[B] {
  values.mapped(transform)
}
```

`over` is written **once** and serves `Array` and `Std.Tree`.

## The design, and what it deliberately excludes

**Arity is written, never inferred.** `F[_]` takes one argument, `F[_, _]` two, a
bare `T` none. Inferring it from use would let the declaration stop saying what
the parameter is, and report a conflict at whichever use came second.

**Only the decidable fragment.** Unification solves a parameter against a
constructor of the same arity and its arguments pairwise. A constructor is never
partially applied and never a computation over types — that is admitted by
construction rather than by a solver that gives up, which is what keeps a
mismatch about two constructors instead of two unsolved shapes.

Excluded, each for its own reason in the ADR: functional dependencies,
associated types, partial application, and kind inference. Kinds here are
arities, not a kind language.

**An unbounded parameter stays opaque.** It says how many arguments its
constructor takes and never which constructor it is. This is refused, correctly:

```pudu
fn read[F[_], A](value: F[A]) -> Array[A] { value.keys() }   // E3005
```

## Proof it carries its weight

The issue's own acceptance asked for standard-library abstractions collapsed
onto it, "to prove the feature carries its weight rather than only
type-checking". `Std.Mappable` does that — `over` and `filled` written once,
serving `Array` and `Std.Tree`, verified running.

`test-fixtures/stdlib/UsesHigherKinds.pudu` is 12 checks, and every one goes
through a definition that **names no container** — a function copied per
container would pass none of them.

## `Option` is deliberately absent, and why

A trait implemented for a **sum** checks and then cannot be called: the value is
a variant, and the member is looked for on `Some` rather than on `Option`.

I verified this is pre-existing and unrelated — a plain non-higher-kinded
`impl Named for Option[Int]` fails identically on `dev`. Filed separately. Until
a variant finds what its own sum implements, an `Option` implementation here
would be a member no caller could reach, so shipping it would be worse than its
absence.

## Blast radius

`Type` gains one constructor; `TypeParam` and `Scheme` carry an arity. That
threaded through ~20 signatures across the checker. `-Werror` with
`-Wincomplete-patterns` found every case needing a decision, and the semantic
sites — substitution, the occurs check, zonking, unification, and method
resolution through a bound — were each handled explicitly rather than left to a
catch-all.

## Validation

`-Werror` at `-O2`, suite at `-O2`, `fmt --check`, 105 diagnostic codes, both
LSP tests, doc-site parity. Eight new checker properties cover solving against
two different constructors, the carried argument still being checked, both
wrong-arity refusals, opacity, and a trait abstracting over the constructor.

## Wiki parity

`ADR-0014`; `grammar/pudu` — the sentence recording that v1 has no higher-kinded
types is **rewritten**, not left contradicting the implementation;
`decisions/_MOC`; new `Std Mappable` page; `Std/_MOC`; `architecture/STDLIB`;
and `CHANGELOG`.

## Review

This is a semantic and public-surface change to the type system and wants
Language Architect review of the arity design, the unification fragment, and the
exclusions — and Forensic Guardian review of source/wiki parity. `AGENTS.md` is
explicit that an implementation author cannot be its sole reviewer.

author: kh-varun
body:
## Summary
- The previous fix (PR #40) made a `nextFixtures` entry stay a polling candidate indefinitely instead of expiring after a fixed 3h window - but that alone doesn't guarantee the match's finish gets detected. The "was live, now isn't" transition check only fires by comparing against `existing` (the previously-live matches this script itself observed) - if the match's *entire* kickoff-to-full-time window falls inside one cron gap, it's never captured as live even once, so `existing` stays empty and the transition never fires.
- Confirmed live: Aston Villa v Arsenal (kickoff 19:00) was still sitting in `nextFixtures` as an upcoming fixture almost 4 hours later. The only two `live-scores.yml` runs that straddled its window landed at 18:07 (before kickoff) and 22:45 (long after full time) - both saw `existing` as empty, so the run at 22:45 correctly found nothing currently live and just... did nothing.

author: braianj
body:
The Explore grid sent no order params, so `/destinations` fell back to its `like_score`
default and the grid was ordered by curation: the highlighted set first, then ranking.
Scenes with people in them sat below featured entries with nobody in them. The in-world
explorer already avoids this by asking for `most_active`; the web did not.

`GetDiscoverDestinationsArgs` now accepts `order_by`, the URL builder forwards it, and the
Explore grid asks for `most_active`. It is passed through rather than defaulted, so the
Featured rail (`only_highlighted`) and My Places (`owner`) keep the curated order they want.

The comment claiming the endpoint silently ignores `order_by` was wrong and is removed. The
endpoint accepts it. The reason the parameter looked inert is that in production curation
outranks the live user count, so the sort term never gets to apply.

**Depends on decentraland/places#868.** Until that ships, this change is inert in production:
`most_active` returns the same list as the default. Safe to merge in either order, but it does
nothing on its own.

### How to test

1. Open Discover and inspect the `/destinations` request for the Explore grid. It should carry
   `order_by=most_active`.
2. The Featured rail and My Places requests should carry no `order_by`.
3. Against a places deployment that has #868 (`.zone`), the grid should lead with scenes that
   have live users, and highlighted-but-empty scenes should fall below them.

author: bspeelm
body:
Part 2 of `docs/plan-0.1.4.md`.

`bothy.lock` pins nine tools and nothing noticed when one moved.

### Why not just run `bothy lock`

It's the only thing that compares a pin against upstream — but it does so as
a side effect of `Relock`, which downloads **every asset for all four
platforms** (~500 MB) because a checksum has to come from the bytes bothy
will actually run. That's right, and useless for a weekly check.

It also **returns nil when every tool fails**, so a workflow could neither
use its exit code nor trust its silence.

### `bothy outdated`

Nine API calls, no asset bytes, about a second. Every piece was already
exported; nothing had composed them.

```
$ bothy outdated
all 9 tools are at their latest release.
```

**A failed check is reported as unknown, not current.** That's the
distinction that matters: a job saying everything's fine because GitHub was
rate-limiting it is worse than one saying nothing. Exit is zero either way —
being out of date is a fact, not a failure, and a scheduled run that goes red
weekly is a run nobody reads.

`LatestRelease` now sends a `User-Agent` (GitHub asks) and a token when set
(lifts the 60/hr limit a shared runner IP otherwise burns on someone else's
behalf). `APIBase` is a variable so tests point it at a local server.

### The workflow

Weekly + `workflow_dispatch`, opening or updating **one** issue — never a PR.
PLAN.md §11 lists auto-updaters as a non-goal, and `lock.go` says why the
lockfile is regenerated deliberately: *"an installer that quietly moves its
own pins is an installer whose output nobody can reproduce."* A bot that
opens a PR is one merge away from being that installer.

One issue *edited*, not one per week, or the tracker fills with
near-identical issues nobody closes. It closes itself when everything is
current again, and creates its own label so this works in a fork with no
setup.

### Verified

Five unit tests against a local forge, including the rate-limited case and
the header/token assertions. The `jq` filters were checked against real
output and against a fixture with one stale and one unknown tool (→ 1, 1).
Ran live: 9 tools, all current.

Code 4048 → 4156, budget 5000.

author: amaadmartin
body:
Please ensure you have read the contribution guide before creating a pull request.

### Link to Issue or Description of Change

1. Link to an existing issue (if applicable):
   No issue.
2. Or, if no issue exists, describe the change:

**Problem**: `adk-js` has no `APIHubToolset`, so an API whose specification lives in API Hub cannot become agent tools unless the caller fetches and parses the specification. `adk-python` has the module and covers it with 7 unit tests.

**Solution**: This change ports `APIHubToolset`, driven by those 7 tests. The tests landed first, red, then the implementation. `APIHubToolset` owns only the three things `OpenAPIToolset` does not: when the specification is fetched, that it is fetched once, and where `name` and `description` come from. The rest delegates to `OpenAPIToolset`.

Two deliberate differences from `adk-python`:

`getSpecContent` returns `Promise<string>`, because a TypeScript HTTP client is asynchronous where Python's `requests` client is not. Local convention wins for that process-internal mechanism. Every observable behaviour is preserved: the eager path starts the fetch in the constructor, `lazyLoadSpec` defers it to the first `getTools()`, and the fetch happens once per instance. The constructor never throws for specification reasons. On the eager path it holds a failure and rethrows it from `getTools()`, so a failed fetch cannot surface as an unhandled rejection.

`apihubClient` is required, and there are no `accessToken` or `serviceAccountJson` options. Python defaults to building an `APIHubClient` from credentials. Shipping those options without the client behind them would be config nobody reads, and shipping an untested HTTP client is worse. The real client is a separate parity item, in flight as `#1340`. It implements this same `BaseAPIHubClient` interface at the same path, so it drops in without a move.

`toSnakeCase` went into `core/src/utils/case_utils.ts` next to `camelCaseKeys`, not into the apihub module. It is a generic string helper, and the guidelines put those in shared utils.

Collision check: `gh pr list` and a title search found `#1341` (`feat/apihub-toolset-module`) and `#1340` (`feat/apihub-client-parity`), both against `main`. This branch is based on `experiment/test-driven-parity` (`e7fab376`), which carries no apihub source or test, and no other PR targets that branch.

### Testing Plan

Please describe the tests that you ran to verify your changes. This is required for all PRs that are not small documentation or typo fixes.

Unit Tests:

- [x] I have added or updated unit tests for my change.
- [x] All unit tests pass locally.

The 7 translated cases are unchanged from when they were written against the absent module. I added two `close()` cases and eight `toSnakeCase` cases for code this change ships. No existing test was deleted or weakened; the `camelCaseKeys` cases in `case_utils_test.ts` are untouched.

Commands run on the pushed commit:

- `npx vitest run --project unit:core core/test/tools/apihub_tool/apihub_toolset_test.ts core/test/utils/case_utils_test.ts` — 23 passed.
- `npx vitest run --project unit:core core/test/tools/openapi_tool core/test/utils` — 508 passed, so the delegate did not regress.
- `npm run ts:check`, `npm run lint`, `npm run format:check`, `npm run docs:check` — all pass.

Coverage of the new source, measured with `--coverage.include` on those files: `apihub_toolset.ts` and `case_utils.ts` are both 100% for statements, branches, functions and lines. `clients/apihub_client.ts` measures 0%. It declares one interface and nothing else, so TypeScript erases the file and there is no runtime code to execute, but v8 still reports its line 1. I did not add a coverage suppression to hide this.

**Proving the tests can fail.** I mutated each behaviour once and recorded which case died:

| Mutation                                         | Failing case                                                                    |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Never fetch eagerly                              | `generates tools from the spec...`                                              |
| `this.preparation` reassigned instead of reused  | `defers the spec fetch...`, client called twice                                 |
| Title fallback `'unnamed'` becomes `''`          | `falls back to "unnamed"...`                                                    |
| `toSnakeCase` call removed                       | `generates tools...` and `snake-cases the title...`                             |
| YAML parse error swallowed                       | `latches an eager spec failure...`                                              |
| Empty-spec early return removed                  | `returns no tools when the spec content is empty`                               |
| Description falls back to the title              | `snake-cases the title...`                                                      |
| Wrong argument passed to `getSpecContent`        | `generates tools from the spec...`                                              |
| Operations dropped from the parsed spec          | three cases, including the auth case                                            |
| Eager rejection left unlatched                   | `latches an eager spec failure...`, run exits 1 on an unhandled `YAMLException` |
| `close()` stops tolerating an unprepared toolset | `closes a toolset that never loaded a spec`                                     |
| Each `toSnakeCase` rule, removed in turn         | one to six `toSnakeCase` cases each                                             |

One mutation survived, and it found dead code rather than a missing test. Removing `.replace(/_+/g, '_')` from `toSnakeCase` failed nothing. The earlier `[^a-zA-Z0-9]+` already collapses runs, and the two camelCase rules only insert an underscore between two alphanumeric characters, so a repeated underscore never reaches that rule. I deleted the rule instead of writing a test for an unreachable line. `adk-python` carries the same unreachable statement; the output is identical either way.

Manual End-to-End (E2E) Tests:

There is no live end-to-end test. Reaching real API Hub needs a project and credentials, and the HTTP client that would use them is not part of this change. The toolset's contract is exercised through an injected `BaseAPIHubClient`, which is the seam a real client plugs into.

### Checklist

- [x] I have read the CONTRIBUTING.md document.
- [x] I have performed a self-review of my own code.
- [x] I have commented my code, particularly in hard-to-understand areas.
- [x] I have added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works.
- [x] New and existing unit tests pass locally with my changes.

author: henryj41043
body:
## Summary
- Bug (user-reported): after picking an option, editing the text (deleting characters, or clearing it) no longer narrowed the dropdown — the list stayed frozen until the dialog was cancelled.
- Root cause (found via an instrumented real-Chromium run): the dialogs bind `[options]` to **getters that build a fresh array every CD cycle**, so `FilterSelect.ngOnChanges` fires on every change-detection pass. Once a selection existed, its unconditional `searchText = selectedLabel` re-resolution reset the text on every keystroke, clobbering the filter. (Before a selection `selectedValue` was null, which is why initial filtering worked — and why the earlier click-fix testing didn't surface this.)
- Fix: `ngOnChanges` re-resolves the displayed label **only when the box still shows the previous options' label** for the selection (the legit late-arriving-options case) — never over in-progress typing.

## Test plan
- [x] New real-Chromium e2e (`e2e/filter-select.e2e.spec.ts`, hermetic mocked API): login → reminder dialog → type `jos` → click-pick Josh Henry → delete to `Jo` → list narrows again → clear → full list → filter `casey` → second pick lands. Reproduced the bug before the fix; 5×/5 green after.

author: featurecreep-cron
body:
## Symptom

PR #59 merged cleanly and then **nothing ran**. Its resulting develop HEAD (`cdcfbab`) has zero workflow runs against it:

```
22:59  Dependency Graph / Scorecard / CI / CodeQL / Docker   sha=8d39d700   <- #58, merged by hand
22:31  Dependency Graph / Scorecard / CI / CodeQL / Docker   sha=7d24a0d6   <- #57, merged by hand
       (nothing at all)                                      sha=cdcfbab3   <- #59, auto-merged
```

## Cause

GitHub does not start new workflow runs for events triggered by `GITHUB_TOKEN`. `automerge.yml` enabled auto-merge with it, so the merge landed and the pipeline stopped there silently.

#57 and #58 triggered builds only because I merged those by hand with a PAT. The moment auto-merge did its job, post-merge CI stopped — which is exactly the state the new pipeline is meant to run in.

On `main` this would be worse: a promotion that builds no image and triggers no release, with no error anywhere.

## Fix

Use the app installation token, which does cascade. The job already mints one to post the approving review, so this adds no new credential or permission.

## Note

This also means the Docker fix in #59 is still **unverified** — no build has run against it. The next merge will be its first real test.

author: steipete
body:
## What problem does this PR solve?

The target-normalization suite resets the entire module graph and reloads the same owner before each of its 23 cases. It also imports unused real registry exports through a partial mock.

## Why this approach?

Load the owner once and advance the mocked registry version between fixtures, using the cache invalidation contract that production already owns. The existing cache test now changes the generation between its cache-hit and replacement observations. The generation stays monotonic across the suite, so fixtures cannot accidentally reuse a previous normalizer. Use the exact loaded-plugin lookup mock already used by the target-resolver sibling.

## User impact

Test-only cleanup: production +0/-0; tests +17/-35. This removes 23 module-graph resets and 22 repeated owner evaluations while keeping all 23 cases and their assertions. No cache-reset production export is added.

## Evidence

All 49 selected tests pass before and after: 23 normalization cases, 20 target-resolver cases and six real channel-registry cases. Full changed-file checks and Codex autoreview pass. The selected proof retains registry invalidation, prepared-plugin partitioning, directory fallback, reserved targets and real registry replacement.

`pnpm test src/infra/outbound/target-normalization.test.ts`

`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/outbound/target-resolver.test.ts`

`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/channels/plugins/registry.test.ts`

Uncontrolled local command timings were 5.60 s before and 6.20 s after, with roughly unchanged RSS; the after run overlapped other validation. No elapsed-time speedup is claimed. The demonstrated improvement is simpler fixture ownership and removal of repeated module work.

author: marchand884
davidbshan
body:
## What

Raise `max_num_seqs` from 8 to 32 on all three hosted serving tiers, from a real B200 sweep.
Also corrects three KV token counts that were wrong on `dev`, and replaces a stale justification
for `MAX_INPUTS`.

## Why

All three tiers inherited `max_num_seqs = 8` from the cards they used to run on (L40S / H100 /
H200). Since PR #1376 moved them to B200 the value was never re-measured, and it was binding:
doubling offered load past the cap bought almost nothing while TTFT rose ~9x.

| tier | throughput at 2x cap | p50 TTFT at 2x cap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 9B | +0.7% | 0.054s -> 0.511s (9.5x) |
| 27B | +1.1% | 0.170s -> 1.532s (9.0x) |
| 35B | +1.7% | 0.220s -> 1.583s (7.2x) |

That is the cap-bound signature: requests past the cap queue inside the container rather than run.

## Measurements

One boot per cap value, five load cells per boot, `n=1` and `n=4`, on a separate bench app
(`flash-serving-capacity-bench`) -- never production. Zero request errors in all 9 cells.
Throughput is container tok/s at each cap's OWN capacity.

| tier | 8 | 16 | 32 | gain |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 9B | 2165 | 3307 | **4793** | 2.2x |
| 27B | 721 | 1110 | **1899** | 2.6x |
| 35B | 721 | 1200 | **3196** | 4.4x |

32 is a measured knee, not just the largest value tried: headroom remaining above the cap
collapses to +2.2% (9B), +3.1% (27B), +10.1% (35B), so 64 would buy little -- and 64 is
independently ruled out, the earlier B200/B300 sweep saw a 4x regression and a hang there.

Latency does not regress. The 35B's p50 TTFT actually **improves** at 32 (0.553s -> 0.463s):
a cap that fits the card removes queueing rather than adding it.

`n=4` fan-out (one request -> four sequences) is the worst case at cap 32 and behaves the same
as plain concurrency: 9B 4739 t/s at 0.198s, 27B 2030 t/s at 0.444s, 35B 2645 t/s at 0.303s.

## Memory

No cost. Free VRAM is flat across the whole range on every tier (9B ~18.4 GiB, 27B ~18.2, 35B
18.11 -> 17.77) and the KV pool moves 0.07% / 0.13% / 0.24%. The 35B is the OOM-fragile tier and
its config comment held the cap at 8 out of concern that startup memory profiling (which runs
`max_num_seqs` sequences) would spike on 248k-vocab logits plus all-expert MoE activations.
Measured, that concern does not bind at 32: zero OOM or preemption lines in any log. The comment
now records the measurement rather than the concern.

## Boot

`max_num_seqs` is part of the vLLM compile-cache key, so **the first boot after this change
recompiles once per tier**, then later boots are warm. Expect one slow cold boot per tier on
deploy. The 27B's 948s cold boot at 32 is 430s of `torch.compile` plus 161s of Dynamo transform;
warm it is ~518s. Worst boot measured anywhere in the sweep is 948s against a 2700s
`STARTUP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`.

(Boot time tracks cache state, not cap value. The 27B boots came out non-monotonic -- 392s at 8,
202s at 16, 948s at 32 -- and the cheap ones are exactly the ones that print
`Directly load the compiled graph`. The 35B's cap-32 boot was cache-warm at 362s, faster than its
cold 657s boot at 16.)

## Also in this change

- **Three KV token counts on `dev` are wrong** and are corrected: 9B 7,109,793 -> 8,713,056;
  35B 3,678,952 -> 5,177,120; 27B 2,856,884 -> 3,691,072. They came from vLLM's
  `GPU KV cache size:` console line, which reads 1.23-1.41x under the resolved allocator.
  Independently confirmed: dividing the GiB figures already on `dev` (a different source) by the
  corrected counts gives 16,374 / 32,773 / 10,241.5 bytes per token -- 2^14, 2^15, and 10,240,
  each within 0.08%. The console-line values reconcile to nothing.
- **`MAX_INPUTS = 64` keeps its value but loses a stale justification.** It cited
  `scripts/gpu_canary.py` on A10G/Qwen2.5-1.5B -- a different card, a model smaller than the
  smallest hosted tier, and a script that no longer exists on `dev`. It now cites this sweep. It
  binds nothing today (every tier authors its own cap); it is a ceiling and a fallback.
- **`max_num_seqs` is removed from `_CATALOG_CHECKED_FIELDS`** in customer-owned
  `flash/serve`. Those profiles are live-qualified on L40S/H100/H200, where a B200-measured depth
  of 32 is unmeasured -- and an L40S is a 48 GiB card. This is the same shape-vs-placement split
  PR #1376 made for `modal_gpu`: the card and how deeply it is packed travel together, and neither
  is a promise the catalog makes to a caller. Engine SHAPE is still enforced. The test replaces the
  removed assertion with a per-model pin on BOTH sides (not a weaker "they differ"), verified by
  sabotage: drifting the 9B customer profile 8 -> 32 fails it.

## Validation

- `tests/serving/`, `tests/test_catalog_consistency.py`, and every customer-serve profile suite: clean.
- `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `check_file_size.py`, `check_function_size.py`: clean.
- Derived concurrency verified end to end: all three tiers admit 32, scale out at 24, share
  `LoraEngine_B200_c32`.
- Full offline suite at the publication boundary.

author: hungchistudio-glitch
body:
## The reported problem

The camera ran out of recognitions almost immediately. It did, and production
says so: `ai_usage_daily` shows a reader stopped at exactly **15**
`vision_identification` at 18:46 UTC today. The all-time peak across every
row in that table is also 15 — the cap was never a safety margin, it was the
ceiling itself.

## Why the real number was smaller than fifteen

**Failures were charged like answers.** The unit is spent before the model
runs — the only ordering that is safe when two shutter presses race — and it
was never given back when the call failed.

**And the failures were manufactured here.** Written out, the arithmetic
could not work:

| | |
|---|---|
| per model attempt | 8s |
| model candidates | 2 |
| browser abort | 16s |

8 + 8 = 16. The fallback model **could not once have delivered an answer to a
reader**: when the first attempt timed out there were zero seconds left, and
the browser gave up at exactly the moment the fallback would have spoken. All
it could do was hold the request open — after the allowance had been charged.

A low-confidence first answer took the same path. It is kept, the stronger
model is tried, and six seconds plus eight put that reader past the abort
too — so a usable word already in hand was thrown away for one that arrived
after nobody was listening.

Each of those cost a unit and produced nothing, and the reader retried. That
is most of the gap between fifteen and what an afternoon actually bought.

**A third thing, not the reported symptom.** Six routes carried six copies of
the quota accounting, and four had drifted to answering `true` when the
counter was unreachable — no limit at all, at the one moment nothing else is
enforcing one.

## What changed

- **`lib/ai/dailyQuota.ts`** — one implementation of consume and refund,
  replacing six. The in-memory fallback now actually counts everywhere.
- **Refunds**, across all six model-backed routes.
- **A budget for the whole recognition** instead of a stopwatch per attempt:
  20s total, each attempt gets `min(12s, remaining)`, and an attempt is not
  started when what is left would not finish one — better to return the
  imperfect answer than to spend the rest of the budget failing to improve
  it. The client abort moves to 25s so it sits *above* the server's budget
  rather than inside it.
- **The caps:**

  | operation | before | after | override ceiling |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `vision_identification` | 15/day | **60/day** | 100 → 500 |
  | `menu_scan` | 20/day | **40/day** | 100 → 200 |

  Both stay overridable by env var, so raising them further needs no code.

## Why this is free

The fifteen was self-imposed. Gemini's free allowance is per *project* and
shared across readers, in the hundreds of requests a day for flash-lite; two
readers at fifteen were using a rounding error of it. On the free tier
exceeding it produces a 429, not a bill, and this app already handles that
with a model cooldown, a fallback and a "busy" message.

> If the Gemini key has billing enabled, a higher cap does mean higher spend.
> That is the one thing this change cannot decide on its own.

## Migration

`20260831225716_ai_quota_refund` — **already applied to production**, and
verified to match `consume_ai_daily_quota` on every security property:
security definer, pinned `search_path`, `anon` denied, `authenticated`
granted, `PUBLIC` denied. An unauthenticated call raises 42501.

## Verification

`tsc --noEmit` clean · lint clean (1 pre-existing warning in `profile/page.tsx`)
· **754 tests pass**, 17 of them new.

Both new suites were mutation-checked. Removing the budget guard fails
exactly the three budget cases and no others; removing the in-memory refund
fails exactly the two that cover it.

`npm run build` was not run locally — the sandbox declined it. Vercel's own
build on this PR is the check that matters.

## Not done, on purpose

The search-sheet camera still has no localStorage cache while the capture
screen does. With refunds in place a retry costs latency rather than
allowance, and that code was only just stabilised — worth its own change.

author: ericbstie
body:
Fixes #4.

## The problem

Ticking was one-way. `tickField` only ever called `check()`, `stampTick` only ever drew a mark on, and `foldToggles` folded the log down to "boxes touched an odd number of times" — which is only "boxes that should end up ticked" if every box started clear. Nothing established that. Clicking a box that arrived ticked drew the app's own tick over the file's, and there was no way to reach the state the user wanted.

## The change

A `Box` now carries `ticked`: the state the file was found holding it in.

- **`pdf.ts`** reads it off the widget — a checkbox is on when its `fieldValue` is the `exportValue` its own appearance uses for being on.
- **`edits.ts`** folds a toggle against that starting point. `Marks` gains `unticks`: boxes found ticked and since flipped. `ticks` stays what it was, boxes to put a mark in.
- **`export.ts`** clears the field (`uncheck()`), and pdf-lib redraws the widget's appearance on save.
- **`render.ts`** covers the inside of the box on the canvas, since the tick the file arrived with is painted into the page image itself. The outline is left alone — it is not part of the tick.

## Scope: printed boxes stay add-only

The issue asked for this to be decided rather than assumed. Clearing reaches an AcroForm field and no further: that tick is the file's own to redraw, whereas painting white over somebody's scan is a different kind of edit from adding ink to it.

Nothing is lost by that. `findCheckboxes` recognises a printed square by having nothing inside it (`INTERIOR_INK`), so a flat box is never found ticked in the first place — a flat box's second click removes the app's own tick, which already worked. An `untick` aimed at a flat box paints nothing, and there is a test pinning that.

## Tests

- `edits.test.ts`: a box found ticked lands in `unticks` and not `ticks`; a second toggle leaves it as the file had it; `marksOnPage` splits `unticks` by page.
- `export.test.ts`: a form checkbox the file arrived ticked comes out of the save cleared; a printed checkbox is never painted over to clear it (paint ops unchanged).
- `checkbox.spec.ts`: clicking a box the file arrived ticked leaves exactly the dark pixels of the box beside it that was never ticked — the outline and nothing else; and the saved file has the field cleared.
- `fixtures.ts`: `buildFormCheckboxPdf(["agree"])` builds the part-filled form these need.

Unit suite 103 pass, e2e 89 pass, `bun run typecheck` clean.

## What

The home page described the editor in six one-line cards and showed none of it. It now carries a **twelve-section tour of the studio**, each section with a real screenshot of the surface it describes, plus a full-window overview at the top and a jump navigation.

| # | Section | Capture |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | Controls — the generated parameter form | the inspector with a group unfolded |
| 02 | Modulation — binding a parameter to a live source | the modulation popover, bound to `Audio · Bass` |
| 03 | Mixer — several drivers on one parameter | the Interactive mixer, Audio / Hands / Face |
| 04 | Elements — the 17 layer kinds | the add-layer palette |
| 05 | Layers — the content rail | the layers list |
| 06 | Slides — the deck of variants | the filmstrip, five variants |
| 07 | Transitions — montage slides | the transition band, montage on |
| 08 | Export — the variant table | the export dialog with four queued outputs |
| 09 | Transport — the scrubber and clock | the transport bar |
| 10 | Presentation — three axes, five presets | the presentation menu |
| 11 | Document — undo, import, export, share | the rail's document row |
| 12 | Sound — the panel's click synth | the UI-sound settings |

The capabilities grid stays as the tour's table of contents; five of its cards now link to the section that shows what they claim.

## How

- **`StudioFeatures` is a server component handed to `HomePage` through a `studioFeatures` prop**, not imported by it — `HomePage` is `"use client"`, and importing the tour there would ship a dozen sections of static prose to the browser. The whole tour is in the first HTML response.
- **The copy lives in `features.ts` as data**, so the rendered sections, the jump navigation and the `ItemList` JSON-LD cannot drift apart.
- **Captures are screenshots of the running production build**, taken headlessly, converted to 2× WebP with `sharp` and rendered at half size — ~330 KB for the whole set. They were taken with the plugin flags the published image uses (`INTERACTION_BINDINGS=true`): the modulation UI does not exist without it.

## SEO

- The home page gets its own `HOME_DESCRIPTION` instead of the site-wide one.
- `APP_FEATURE_LIST` (the `WebApplication` JSON-LD) is rewritten from the real feature set — it still advertised an EXIF overlay that no longer exists.
- An `ItemList` JSON-LD block describes the tour.
- **`/` is added to `sitemap.ts`**, where it was missing entirely.

## Accessibility

Audited with `axe-core` in both colour schemes, after scrolling `main` to the bottom so every lazy image has loaded: **zero violations**.

- Figures use `<figure>` / `<figcaption>` with alt text describing the panel's content, and intrinsic `width`/`height` so nothing reflows.
- Height caps above `sm` stop a tall inspector from filling the viewport; on a phone the cap is dropped so a UI panel's labels stay readable.
- Text-dense captures (the export table, the transport bar) keep their natural size on a phone inside a focusable, labelled horizontal scroller — the page body never scrolls sideways.
- The one violation the page did have is fixed too: a sketch card printed its name both as alt text and as visible text inside the same link (`image-redundant-alt`), so `AnimatedPreview` takes an `alt` override and the home page's cards pass `""`. The same defect remains in `SketchesList` (the `/sketches` gallery) and is recorded as an open item rather than folded into this change.

## Verification

- `npm run check` (lint + typecheck + test) — clean, 1955 tests passing.
- `npm run build` — clean.
- Rendered and screenshotted at 1400px and 390px, in dark and light themes: no horizontal overflow, anchors land 96px below the top (`scroll-mt-24`), every capture loads.
- `axe-core` audit: 0 violations, dark and light.

## Memory

`docs/memory/home-and-seo.md` is new: how the tour is wired, how to retake the captures, and the traps involved — chiefly that `page.screenshot()` never resolves on a running sketch until playback is paused, and that a default build has no modulation UI to photograph.

author: nemanjan00
body:
bwm_autooff_check() released the power latch on the first VUSB-absent sample, ~250ms after VBUS was pulled. With a BWM fitted that lands while the AW32001E is still transitioning into Battery Discharge Mode, where BATFET is only turned fully on as part of that transition. The board powered down mid-transition and could then not be brought back up by button or by USB insertion - it looked dead until the cell was physically re-inserted.

Require the absence to persist for 5s (20 consecutive 250ms samples) before acting, resetting the count whenever USB reappears. This is the grace period the function's own comment already described, and it also means a single spurious low reading on PC2 - a floating input, configured GPIO_PULL_NONE - can no longer power down a working device.

The 5s figure is empirical rather than derived from a datasheet settling time. Other users report auto-off working on their boards, so this makes a marginal path robust rather than fixing something broken everywhere.

author: alanvaa06
body:
The narrative documentation was already strong. The **reference** documentation did not exist.

A caller wanting to know what `run_backtest` takes, whether `cost_bps` is charged per side or round-trip, or which exception means "your mandate is impossible" had to read the source. This closes that in three pieces.

No behaviour changed, no signature moved. **837 tests pass unchanged**, ruff clean.

---

## What was actually missing

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| API reference | none — no sphinx/mkdocs/pdoc, no site, no `docs/API.md` | 82 generated pages, published from `main` |
| Docstring coverage (677 public defs) | 74.6% — 166 with none | **100%** |
| Functions documenting their parameters | 86 | **379** |
| Functions that raise and declare it | 67 of 364 raise sites | **all** |
| Central error reference | none, across 21 exception classes | `docs/ERRORS.md` |

## 1. A generated API reference

`scripts/build_api_docs.py` renders every public module with pdoc, behind a new `docs` extra. `.github/workflows/docs.yml` builds it on every pull request and publishes it to GitHub Pages from `main`.

Two decisions worth flagging:

- **It runs `--strict`**, which refuses to skip a module it cannot import. Without that, a missing extra would silently drop `mcp_server` from the published pages while the job stayed green — the exact failure mode a generated reference is supposed to eliminate. The job installs `[all,ui,mcp,docs]` on 3.12 for that reason (the MCP SDK needs 3.10+).
- **Modules are discovered by walking the package**, not enumerated, so a new one is documented the day it lands. Private modules are excluded, and a post-build check fails if fewer than 40 pages render — pdoc exits 0 on an empty render otherwise.

pdoc rather than Sphinx because there is nothing to author: the reference is a projection of the docstrings, so the only file that can go stale is one that does not exist.

## 2. `docs/ERRORS.md` — the refusal contract

The engine's whole argument is that it refuses rather than fails obscurely. Leaving the refusal contract undocumented was the expensive irony.

289 lines covering:

- All **21 exception types**, grouped by what they actually mean: *your inputs are wrong* (fix them, retrying is pointless) / *your mandate is impossible* (relax something, the exception says which) / *the world got in the way* (retry, or fix the environment).
- The full `IngestError` hierarchy with **what the service does about each subclass** — retries `ProviderTransientError`, drops the identifier on `IdentifierNotFoundError`, aborts the whole run on `ProviderCredentialsError` because every other identifier would fail identically.
- **CLI exit codes**, and the one case where `--json` changes them: an escaping exception exits `1` with an error payload rather than dying with a traceback on empty stdout.
- A closing section on **what does *not* raise** and is easy to miss with only a `try` block: degraded cost models, skipped identifiers (`result.is_complete`), post-solve constraint breaches, data-quality findings.

## 3. Docstrings, treated as the reference's source

Since the reference is generated from them, docstrings are now part of the public surface rather than a courtesy — `AGENTS.md` says so explicitly.

Parameter docs carry **units where a number has any**, which is where most of the real ambiguity lived:

- `cost_bps` per side vs round-trip
- `execution_lag` in bars, and why a negative one is refused
- `alpha` as a tail probability, not a confidence level (`0.05` for the 95% CVaR, **not** `0.95`)
- VaR `level` in percent rather than as a fraction
- which figures are annualized and on what basis

## Reviewing this

The diff is 78 files but only three shapes of change: new docstrings, extended docstrings, and the three new files (`scripts/build_api_docs.py`, `.github/workflows/docs.yml`, `docs/ERRORS.md`). Nothing outside a docstring or a comment moved in `src/`.

`docs/ERRORS.md` is the part most worth a careful read — every causal claim in it was checked against the actual `raise` sites rather than written from the class names, and a first draft that inferred causes for `SpecValidationError` and `LayerConfigurationError` turned out to be wrong and was corrected.

## One thing before merging

The docs workflow needs **GitHub Pages enabled on the repo with source set to GitHub Actions**, or the `deploy` job will fail on its first run against `main`. The `build` job passes regardless, and pull requests only ever build — they never publish.

author: fedconcas
body:
Stacked on `feat/broker-exclusion-and-classification` (#16), so the diff here is only what is new. Three commits: the review fixes for #16, the follow-up feature work, then the `cleanup-bounces` reconcile.

---

## `06e1e9c` — `cleanup-bounces` clears the address instead of deleting the broker

The CLI and the web UI disagreed about what a bounce means. The web scan clears the dead address and keeps the company; `cleanup-bounces --remove` deleted the whole entry through `RemoveByEmail`, throwing away its name, category, website and opt-out URL and silently shrinking the shipped database — for a company that is still very much alive and simply changed its privacy address.

Both doors now go through `broker.MarkEmailUnreachable`, so a cleared broker keeps everything but its address, records the dropped address and the bounce wording in its notes, and shows up in `list-brokers --missing-email` ready to be given a working one. `RemoveByEmail` had no other caller and is gone.

`cleanup-bounces` also picks up the **hard-bounce gate** the web path uses: a full mailbox or a greylisting deferral is reported as a temporary failure and left alone rather than costing a live broker its address. Previously `--remove` acted on anything the classifier called a bounce. The dry-run and summary lines say which happened, so "nothing was changed" is never silent. The flag stays `--remove` (renaming would break existing scripts); its help now reads "Clear the dead addresses (the broker entries themselves are kept)".

Landing page: the two case-law notes are both EU/UK matters, so they now sit **inside** the EU/UK section behind a rule rather than as a full-width section under both audiences. The two regions are stacked instead of side by side, since the halves are no longer the same height — and the US half has room to grow.

---

## `ce8a144` — Start Here tab, `us-data-only` stops blocking, self-healing broker list

Three changes, all pointing the same way: most people using this are in the US, and nothing should quietly take a broker off their list.

### Start Here tab (`/welcome`, first in the nav)

The right first move differs sharply by where you live, and neither the dashboard nor the broker table was ever going to say so. The new landing tab does:

- **EU/UK**: erasure is a hard right — but most of these companies hold no file with your name on it. What circulates is a hashed email joined to advertising IDs, and only a handful of companies do that joining, so they are worth the first requests. This section also carries the two case-law notes (the Belgian DPA's IAB Europe TCF ruling; the UK tribunal's Experian decision).
- **US**: no federal erasure right, a state-law patchwork instead; here the file usually *does* exist by name; and two things a deletion request will not do — a credit file is FCRA's, not the CCPA's, and deletion does not stop hash matching. Same identity-resolution list applies.

The identity-resolution table is rendered **from the loaded broker database**, not written into the copy, so a company retired from `brokers.yaml` drops off the page instead of linking nowhere; `TestWelcomeIdentityResolverIDsExist` pins that every ID the page names is still in the shipped data. Each row links into the broker list and to the company's own opt-out form where there is one. The page carries a "Draft copy" badge — the wording is a first pass over supplied material and is the author's to edit.

### `us-data-only` no longer blocks `Sendable()`

It was introduced as a hard block, "same as `b2b-only`". That is backwards for this audience: *"we only hold data on US customers"* describes exactly the broker a US user most needs to write to. It stays a classification — shown on the row, filterable, and the right thing to record when an EU/UK user gets a "no record of you" reply — but it never removes a broker from anyone's send list. `b2b-only` (holds no consumer data) and `form-only` (refuses email) still block, because those are refusals rather than scope.

### The broker list heals itself from bounces

An inbox scan now clears a broker's address when the reply proves it permanently undeliverable, so a dead address stops costing every future send a silent failure — no `cleanup-bounces` run, and no wait for a new release of the shipped data file.

Two gates have to agree, deliberately asymmetric:

1. the classifier says "delivery failed" (`ResponseBounced`), and
2. the new `inbox.IsHardBounce` says the failure is **permanent** — a 5.x.x enhanced status, a 5xx reply code, or wording naming the recipient unknown, **and no transient signal anywhere in the message**. A full mailbox, a greylisting deferral or a "will retry" veto it outright: clearing a live broker's address on a temporary failure would drop it from every future send with nothing to put it back.

The broker is never deleted. `broker.MarkEmailUnreachable` clears the address and records it, plus the bounce wording, in `Notes`; the entry keeps its name, category, website and opt-out URL, still shows under "Include non-sendable", and can be given a working address later. The whole batch goes through one `mutateBrokers` call (one file write per scan) and the scan summary reports what it dropped.

---

## `6eefc40` — Review fixes for #16

### Correctness

- **Lost exclusions.** `handleAPIExcludeBroker` wrote the config with an unsynchronized load-copy-save-store, so two Exclude clicks in flight together each copied the same snapshot and the later save dropped the other's exclusion. Reproduced: 4 concurrent excludes, 1–2 survived. Adds `Server.mutateConfig` (mutex + copy + save + publish), the twin of `mutateBrokers`, and routes every config writer in `internal/web` through it.
- **Clobbered CLI edits.** `mutateBrokers` wrote the startup snapshot back over `brokers.yaml`, silently reverting an `eraser tag-broker` edit made while `serve` was running. It now re-reads the file under `brokerMu`.
- **Atomic writes.** `brokers.yaml` and `config.yaml` are written via temp file + rename (new `internal/fsutil`); both are now rewritten by ordinary UI clicks, and `config.yaml` holds the SMTP/IMAP credentials with no `.bak`.
- **`--timeout` didn't bound DNS.** `MXExists` ignored the caller's context and built its own 15s `context.Background()`.
- **Unguarded outbound fetches.** The audit client re-implemented `internal/browser`'s client without its SSRF guard; now built on `browser.GuardedTransport()`, with one shared UA constant.
- **Dead HEAD→GET fallback** in `WebsiteAlive` that could only downgrade a proven-live site to `unknown`.
- **`setBrokersForTest`** shipped in the production binary and skipped `brokerMu`; moved to `export_test.go`.

### Shared rules, one copy each

`broker.ApplyDisposition` (tag rules, 2 copies → 1) · `broker.ToSet` + `brokerExcluded` (exclusion matching, 5 copies → 1, and only one of them trimmed whitespace) · `handleAPIBrokers` = `renderBrokerListFragment` · one `#broker-filters` container replacing 15 hand-copied `hx-include` lists · `auditOne`'s 8-arm switch (with a provably unreachable `default`) → 5 arms · `audit-brokers --history/--replies` no longer drags a full crawl along · `list-brokers` uses `IsDispositionTag` · duplicate `Tags`/`DispositionTags` render keys → one key.

Also `gofmt`s `internal/history/history.go`, which the CI gofmt check was already failing on (pre-existing, from `183b14c`).

## Test plan

- [x] `go build ./... && go vet ./... && gofmt -l .` clean
- [x] `go test -race ./...` green
- [x] New: hard-vs-soft bounce table (including a 5xx quoted inside a temporary failure staying soft); a scan clearing a hard-bounced address and leaving a soft-bounced one alone, persisted and idempotent on a second pass; `MarkEmailUnreachable` rules; the welcome page rendering from the database; curated resolver IDs present in the shipped data; concurrent excludes all surviving; a web write preserving an out-of-process CLI tag; `ApplyDisposition`; atomic `Save`; `MXExists` honouring a can

author: fpt
body:
`duckdb_open` takes no configuration, so there was no way to open a database read-only through this driver. A process whose only job is to read should not be able to write by accident, and asking the engine to enforce that is worth more than intending it.

Options arrive as a DSN query string and go through `duckdb_open_ext`:

```go
sql.Open("duckdb", "warehouse.duckdb?access_mode=READ_ONLY&threads=2")
```

`NewDuckDBWithSettings(path, settings)` is the direct form. `NewDuckDB(path)` is unchanged and delegates to it.

## DSN rules

- **A path with no `?` takes the original `duckdb_open` path** unchanged, so nothing existing changes behaviour.
- **The last `?` separates**, not the first. A DuckDB path may legitimately contain one, and taking the first would make such a file unopenable with no way to say otherwise. A path whose name ends in `?` is written `./odd?name.duckdb?`.
- **An unrecognised option fails the open** with DuckDB's own message rather than being silently dropped. So does a bad value.
- **A repeated option is an error.** `?access_mode=READ_ONLY&access_mode=READ_WRITE` is refused rather than resolved.

That last rule is a change from the original PR, which took the last value silently. DSNs get built by concatenation, so the two halves can come from different parts of a program, and quietly honouring one is how a database asked to be read-only becomes writable. There is no answer that is safe to guess, and nobody writes a duplicate key on purpose, so refusing costs callers nothing.

## Documentation

Both entry points accept every option DuckDB accepts at open time — 299 of them in DuckDB 1.5.5. Some govern extension loading (native code in the process), filesystem and network reach, and machine resources.

The driver applies no allowlist and no denylist. A driver cannot know whether the caller is a trusted ETL job or a multi-tenant query endpoint, and a policy that fits one is wrong for the other. So the README and `docs/CONFIGURATION.md` now lead with:

> **Disclaimer:** go-pduckdb is just glue, not a secure wrapper. Design your own security model when you use this package.

`docs/CONFIGURATION.md` is the reference behind that decision: the DSN parsing rules, and what the open-time options reach, grouped as privileged execution, permission escalation, filesystem and network reach, resource exhaustion, and durability.

## Verification

Every documented behaviour was checked against libduckdb 1.5.5 rather than assumed, including that `enable_external_access` is one-way (`Cannot enable external access while database is running`).

- `TestSplitDSN` — the split, including the awkward paths
- `TestSplitDSNRejectsARepeatedOption` and `TestOpenRejectsARepeatedOption` — refused, and the error reaches a `sql.Open` caller
- `TestReadOnlyRefusesAWrite` — writes to a database, reopens it read-only, reads successfully, and checks the write is refused, so the flag is proven to reach DuckDB rather than merely be passed to it
- `go build`/`go test ./...` pass with `CGO_ENABLED=0`; `golangci-lint run` reports 0 issues

## Credit

The feature and its first commit are Calvin Cheng's, from #39, and that commit keeps their authorship. #39 was closed in error — its author compared against their fork's `main`, where the work had genuinely landed, rather than this repository's. Rebased here onto the correct base, without the fork-maintenance commits it carried (a module rename to `github.com/calvinchengx/go-pduckdb`, a fork README banner, and the deletion of the AI review workflow), which were not intended for this repository.

Closes #39.

author: nightmareftw
body:
## Summary
Root cause of "the Chaos page shows English no matter which language is selected": its curated guide (`scripts/data/vs-curated-guides.js`) was one flat English object with nothing to switch to — a leftover from before the file supported per-language content at all.

The generic `assets/js/i18n.js` DOM-text-node translator can't fix this by itself: most guide items embed a cross-linked character/achievement name via `character.js`'s `linkify()`, which splits the sentence into multiple DOM text nodes around the injected `<a>` tag, so a translated fragment could never exact-match a whole node.

Fixed by giving the guide its own `{en, pt}` pair — the `pt` copy is the original Portuguese text this guide was built from — with an **identical phase/group/item shape** on both sides (verified programmatically), and picking whichever matches `localStorage`'s `nftw:lang` before `linkify()` ever touches it. Since checkbox ids are positional, the identical shape also means progress survives a language switch instead of scrambling.

## Test plan
- [x] EN: Chaos page renders fully in English; checked 2 steps.
- [x] Switched to PT via the flag toggle: page content re-rendered fully in Portuguese, and the same 2 steps stayed checked (`2/93` in both languages).
- [x] Cross-linked character names (proper nouns) render correctly and identically regardless of language.
- [x] Switched back to EN: content and progress both still correct.
- [x] `characters.html`'s "N-step guide" chip on the Chaos card translates correctly in both languages.
- [x] Verified programmatically that the `en` and `pt` guide copies have exactly matching phase/group/item counts (10 phases, same shape) so checkbox ids can never diverge between languages.
- [x] Zero console/page errors in either language.
